## Choosing the best industrial real estate broker in Chicagoland

Match a broker to your property type, size, location and sale goals. Ask any broker, including Pavlo Rospopa:

### How do I find the best commercial real estate broker in Chicago?

Look for regular sales of your property type, size and county. Request recent comparable closings and buyer types, not career volume. Verify Illinois licensing with the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation .

### What makes the best broker for selling an industrial building?

- Industrial investment sales focus. Selling a building to an investor or owner-user is different work from leasing space.
- Buyer reach. Access to private investors, 1031 exchange buyers, and owner-users who buy buildings of your size.
- Pricing you can check. A recommended price supported by comparable sales, rent analysis, and the way buyers will underwrite the building.
- A written process. A marketing plan, confidentiality steps for tenants and employees, and regular reporting on activity and offers.

### What should I ask a commercial real estate broker before signing a listing agreement?

- Which similar buildings have you sold in the last few years, at what prices, and to which kinds of buyers?
- How did you arrive at the recommended price, and what would change it?
- Who will market the property, and how will you protect confidentiality?
- What are the fee, term, and exclusions in the listing agreement?

### Do I need an investment sales broker or a leasing broker?

An investment sales broker prices and markets leased or vacant buildings. A leasing or tenant-representation broker fills vacancies or finds business space. Vacant buildings may attract investors and owner-users; ask how the broker reaches both.

FAQ · Industrial real estate & Chicagoland industrial

# Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered

General education for the Chicagoland market, not advice on any specific property, lease, loan, or tax position. Market figures change quarterly; verify current data before relying on it.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Common industrial real estate questions cover warehouses, leases, investing, selling, diligence, Illinois taxes and zoning, and the Chicago market. Answers start with the short version and link to deeper guides.

- Industrial real estate is property built to make, store, move, or service goods, including warehouses, distribution centers, manufacturing plants, flex buildings, and outdoor storage yards.
- Most industrial leases are net: tenants pay base rent plus their share of taxes, insurance, and common-area costs.
- Value follows documented income, building function (clear height, docks, truck court, power), and location, not price per square foot alone.
- In Illinois, property taxes are often the largest operating expense; Cook County assesses industrial property differently from the collar counties.
- Chicagoland’s rail, interstate, and air connections make it one of North America’s largest and most liquid industrial markets.
- Owner lens: For an operating owner, use each answer as a prompt to verify the specific building, lease, authority, and deadline; general guidance is not proof that a use or improvement is approved at your site.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_A real warehouse interior with pallet racking. Operating fit depends on the actual fleet, equipment, approved use and building conditions._

## Industrial real estate basics

### What is industrial real estate?

Industrial real estate supports manufacturing, storage, distribution and physical goods services: warehouses, fulfillment centers, plants, flex buildings, cold storage, truck terminals and outdoor yards. Unlike office or retail, value depends on function (clear height, loading, truck access, power) and access to highways, rail, labor and customers. See industrial building types and specifications .

### What are the main types of industrial property?

Types include bulk warehouse and distribution, light industrial and small-bay, manufacturing, flex/R&D, cold storage, truck terminals and cross-docks, data centers, specialized facilities and industrial outdoor storage (IOS). Tenant needs and underwriting differ, so specifications matter more than labels. The building types guide compares them.

### What is the difference between a warehouse and a distribution center?

A warehouse mainly stores goods; a distribution center moves them quickly. Inventory turnover in days rather than months typically requires more docks, deeper truck courts, trailer parking, employees and conveyors. Many buildings suit either use; dock count, court depth and parking determine fit.

### What is flex space?

Flex combines finished office or showroom space (often a quarter or more) with warehouse, lab or light assembly space. Usually lower and with more grade-level doors than a warehouse, it suits companies needing offices and goods together. See flex space in the glossary .

### What is small-bay industrial?

Small-bay (or shallow-bay) buildings have suites of a few thousand to roughly 25,000 square feet for contractors, service businesses, distributors and light manufacturers. Suites typically include an office, drive-in or dock door and separate utilities. Limited new construction supports a deep local market for 10,000 to 100,000 SF properties.

### What is a last-mile industrial facility?

A last-mile (or last-touch) warehouse or service building serves final deliveries near dense population. Customer, labor and arterial road access, plus van and fleet parking, outweigh size or height. Chicago and inner-ring suburban infill sites are typical locations.

### What is industrial outdoor storage (IOS)?

IOS land provides truck and trailer parking, equipment staging or material storage, usually fenced, lit, paved or graveled with little or no building. Value depends on zoning, access, surfacing, stormwater compliance and scarcity; many municipalities restrict it. See IOS in the glossary .

### What is cold storage, and why is it different?

Cold storage is a temperature-controlled warehouse for refrigerated or frozen goods. Insulated panels, refrigeration systems, freezer-grade floors with under-slab heating, heavy power, and specialized docks make it far more expensive to build and convert than a dry warehouse. That cost, plus food-safety requirements, keeps supply limited and tenants sticky.

### What do Class A, B, and C mean for industrial buildings?

Class describes age and functionality: A is newer, with modern clear heights, ESFR sprinklers, deep truck courts and wide columns; B is older but functional; C has limits such as low clear height, tight columns or poor access. Classes are not standardized; compare specifications. See industrial building classes .

### Who leases and owns industrial buildings?

Tenants include manufacturers, distributors, third-party logistics (3PL), e-commerce and retail companies, contractors, food and beverage firms and service businesses. Owners include occupying owner-users, private investors, family offices, syndicators, private equity funds, institutions and publicly traded REITs. Owner-users and private investors are the most common 10,000 to 100,000 SF buyers.

## Building specifications

### What is clear height in a warehouse?

Clear height is the distance from the floor to the lowest overhead obstruction, usually roof joists, beams, or sprinkler lines. It sets racking height and storage capacity. Measure the lowest point, not the roof peak. See clear height in the glossary .

### How much clear height does a modern warehouse need?

Modern bulk distribution commonly has mid-30s to 40 feet clear height; functional small-bay and older buildings often have 16 to 24 feet. Racked distribution benefits from height; contractors, service users and light manufacturers may prioritize doors, power and yard. Match likely tenants.

### What is the difference between dock-high and grade-level doors?

A dock-high door aligns with truck-bed height (roughly four feet above the court), letting forklifts enter semi-trailers. A grade-level (drive-in) door lets vehicles and equipment enter from the ground. Distribution users need docks; contractors and service users often need drive-in doors. Many buildings have both. See dock-high door and drive-in door .

### How many dock doors does a warehouse need?

A common distribution rule of thumb is one dock door per 5,000 to 10,000 square feet; cross-dock or parcel operations may need more, long-term storage fewer. Count usable doors with working levelers, seals, and trailer positions, not wall openings.

### What is a truck court, and how deep should it be?

The truck court is the paved maneuvering and parking area before dock doors. Modern single-sided courts commonly measure 120 to 135 feet, with more depth needed when trucks use both sides. Shallow courts limit truck access and are hard to fix. See truck court .

These are screening examples, not safe-clearance guarantees. Review the sourced vehicle dimensions and turning-path reference and have a qualified engineer check the fleet's entry, backing, and exit paths.

### Why does column spacing matter in an industrial building?

Column spacing affects how efficiently racking, aisles, and equipment fit. Wider spacing adds flexibility; tight spacing wastes floor area and may rule out users. Modern buildings commonly use 50-foot bays with deeper speed bays at docks. See column spacing .

### What is an ESFR sprinkler system?

ESFR (early suppression, fast response) is a ceiling sprinkler system designed to suppress high-piled storage fires without in-rack sprinklers in many configurations. Adequacy depends on commodity, storage and building height, and water supply; a fire-protection engineer should confirm fit for each tenant. See ESFR sprinklers .

### How much electrical power does an industrial building need?

Lighting and battery charging may need modest service; manufacturing, cold storage, and EV fleets may need much more. Service is described by amperage, voltage, and phase; three-phase is standard for motors and machinery. Confirm capacity with an electrician and utility, as upgrades can take months. See three-phase power .

### What should I know about the floor slab?

Racking, forklifts and machinery depend on slab thickness, reinforcement, capacity and flatness. Tall racks and narrow-aisle equipment need level floors; heavy manufacturing needs high capacity. Review drawings, cracking and joint failure; have an engineer assess demanding uses. See slab load and flatness .

### How much office space is typical in an industrial building?

Warehouse and distribution buildings often have under 10 to 15 percent office; flex buildings may have more. Excess office raises costs, may sit empty, and narrows the tenant pool. Match office area to local users. See office finish percentage .

## Industrial leases

### How do industrial leases usually work?

Most industrial leases are net: base rent plus tenants' share of taxes, insurance and common-area or maintenance costs. Terms govern rent, length, use, repairs, renewal and move-out. Compare total occupancy cost, not just base rent. See the lease comparison guide .

### What is a triple-net (NNN) lease?

A triple-net lease requires tenants to pay base rent plus their share of property taxes, insurance, and common-area maintenance. It is common for industrial property, but leases differ on roof, structure, parking, and HVAC replacements. Read repair and capital clauses. See NNN in the glossary .

### What is the difference between gross, modified gross, and NNN leases?

In a gross lease, the landlord covers expenses through higher rent. Modified gross splits expenses, such as utilities and increases above a base year. In an NNN lease, tenants pay their share of taxes, insurance, and maintenance in addition to base rent. Compare all-in annual cost. See gross and modified gross .

### What are CAM charges?

CAM (common area maintenance) is a tenant’s share of shared-property costs such as snow removal, landscaping, parking repair, lighting, and sometimes management. Check inclusions, allocations, caps, and capital pass-throughs. See CAM in the glossary .

### How long are industrial leases?

Industrial leases commonly run three to ten years: often three to five for small-bay and small-business tenants, ten or more for large distribution and build-to-suit. Longer terms usually bring more landlord-funded improvements and free rent; shorter terms offer flexibility. Renewal options let tenants extend.

### How do rent escalations work in industrial leases?

Base rent usually rises by a fixed percentage or amount per square foot; some leases use CPI or stepped increases. Escalations compound, so model total rent over the term. See escalations .

### What is a tenant improvement (TI) allowance?

A TI allowance funds tenant build-out or modifications such as offices, electrical, lighting, restrooms, or dock work. Usually quoted per square foot, it reflects lease term and credit and is recovered through rent. Clarify construction management and treatment of unused funds. See TI allowance .

### How is industrial rent quoted?

Industrial rent is usually annual dollars per square foot, net of taxes, insurance and CAM. Smaller suites may quote monthly gross rent. Confirm net or gross, annual or monthly, and request current expense estimates.

### Who pays for the roof, HVAC, and structural repairs in an industrial lease?

The lease controls. Tenants commonly maintain their space and HVAC; landlords retain roof replacement and structure. Some “absolute NNN” leases shift everything to tenants. Distinguish repair and replacement duties and whether replacements can be amortized into CAM.

### What should I ask before leasing a warehouse?

Confirm zoning allows your use; clear height, door types and count, truck-court depth, and trailer parking; electrical service; sprinkler adequacy for your storage; office and restroom count; current taxes, insurance, and CAM; repair and replacement responsibilities; renewal and expansion rights; restoration obligations at move-out; and access hours, security, and outdoor storage rights. The tour checklist covers what to measure.

## Space, rent, and lease-or-buy

### How much warehouse space do I need?

Start with inventory, pallets, racking height, aisles, staging, shipping, equipment, office headcount and growth, plus truck, parking and yard needs. A racking or logistics consultant's efficient layout may need less space than a rough estimate.

### How much does it cost to lease industrial space in the Chicago area?

Chicagoland rent varies by submarket, size, age, clear height, office share, and yard. Small suites and infill locations generally cost more per square foot than large outer-corridor buildings. Budget for taxes, insurance, and CAM, which can be significant in Cook County. Check quarterly brokerage reports and signed comparable leases, not just asking rents.

### What factors drive industrial lease rates?

Location and access, vacancy in the submarket, building size and suite size, clear height, docks and doors, truck court and trailer parking, power, office finish, age and condition, outdoor storage rights, lease term, tenant credit, and improvement allowances. Property taxes also matter because tenants weigh total occupancy cost, not just base rent.

### Should a business lease or buy its industrial building?

Buying offers control, equity, rent-increase protection and a long-term asset, but ties up capital and adds concentration and repair risk. Leasing preserves cash and flexibility. Stable businesses needing specialized improvements may buy with SBA 504 financing; fast-growing firms often lease. Compare the same horizon with your accountant.

### What is a build-to-suit?

A build-to-suit serves a specific tenant or buyer, usually committed before construction. A long lease or purchase commitment secures needed specifications and reduces developer leasing risk. Site selection, entitlements, design and construction often take a year or more.

### What is a speculative (spec) industrial building?

A speculative (spec) building anticipates demand without a signed tenant. Generic modern standards suit many users and permit faster occupancy than build-to-suit, while added supply can affect submarket rents.

### What is an industrial sublease, and is it a good option?

A sublease offers some or all of a tenant's space, usually with landlord consent. It may cost less and include furniture or racking, but cannot exceed the original term and depends on the tenant's good standing. Read the master lease.

### What security deposit or guaranty will an industrial landlord ask for?

Security reflects tenant finances, time in business, lease term, and landlord costs for improvements and commissions. Expect a cash deposit or letter of credit; newer or smaller tenants may also need a personal or corporate guaranty. Negotiate a burn-down after on-time payments.

### Who pays the broker on an industrial lease?

Landlords usually pay leasing commissions under their listing agreement, typically sharing them with the tenant's broker. Arrangements vary; confirm each broker's compensation and required Illinois agency disclosures. See leasing commission .

### What is a letter of intent (LOI) in commercial real estate?

An LOI summarizes price or rent, term, contingencies, timing and conditions before the purchase agreement or lease. Business terms usually do not bind, but confidentiality or exclusivity may. Clear terms reduce surprises. See LOI .

## Investing in industrial

### Is industrial real estate a good investment?

Industrial has performed strongly over the past decade, supported by e-commerce, supply-chain changes, and limited infill supply. Buildings are relatively simple to operate and often net-leased, but returns depend on price, rents, lease terms, rates, and new construction. No property is a good investment at any price. See the investment guide .

### What are the advantages of investing in industrial property?

Advantages can include net leases that pass through operating costs, lower capital spending per square foot than office or retail, invested tenants, a broad user base, and buyer and lender demand. Smaller buildings also attract owner-users, adding exit options.

### What are the main risks of investing in industrial real estate?

Key risks include tenant default and vacancy, rollover concentration, new speculative supply, functional obsolescence, environmental contamination, rising property taxes, capital costs for roofs and pavement, interest-rate and refinancing risk, and zoning limits on use or outdoor storage. Most are identifiable in diligence. See diligence and risk questions .

### How do I start investing in industrial real estate?

Choose public industrial REITs, passive syndications or funds, or direct ownership. Direct buyers often start with a small single-tenant or small-bay building in a familiar market. Assemble a broker, attorney, lender, inspectors and accountant; learn lease and operating statement analysis before offering.

### What is an industrial REIT?

An industrial REIT owns and usually operates industrial properties, distributing most taxable income. Public REITs offer liquidity and diversification, but no individual building control; share prices move with the market. Direct ownership offers control and tax-planning options with less liquidity.

### What do core, value-add, and opportunistic mean?

They describe risk strategies. Core is stabilized, well-located property with long leases and low leverage. Core-plus adds modest upside. Value-add involves leasing up vacancy, renovating, or re-tenanting to raise income. Opportunistic includes development, heavy repositioning, or distressed situations with the highest risk and expected return. See value-add vs. core .

### What is the difference between an owner-user and an investor buyer?

Owner-users buy for occupancy, location, layout and control; investors buy tenant income. Owner-users may pay more for vacant or soon-vacant buildings, especially with SBA 504 financing; investors pay for existing leases. The fitting buyer pool shapes pricing and marketing. See owner-user vs. investor .

### What is a 1031 exchange, and how does it work for industrial property?

A Section 1031 exchange can defer federal capital gains tax when proceeds from an investment property sale are reinvested in another qualifying property. IRS rules generally require identification within 45 days and acquisition within 180 days, with proceeds held by a qualified intermediary. Industrial property may be exchanged for other real property held for investment or business use. Consult a tax advisor. See 1031 exchange .

### What is a sale-leaseback?

A business sells its occupied building to an investor and simultaneously leases it back long term. Equity becomes working capital without moving operations; the buyer gets a known tenant. Rent and lease terms drive price. See the selling guide’s sale-leaseback section .

### How do you finance an industrial property purchase?

Sources include banks, credit unions, life companies, CMBS lenders, debt funds, and SBA 504 or 7(a) loans for owner-users. Lenders test LTV, debt-service coverage, and sometimes debt yield, as well as lease term, tenant credit, and environmental reports. Compare rate, term, amortization, recourse, reserves, and prepayment terms. See financing in the investment guide .

## Valuation and underwriting

### What is a cap rate?

Cap rate is net operating income divided by price or value. A building with $100,000 NOI selling for $1.5 million has a rate of about 6.7 percent. Lower rates mean higher prices relative to income. Check whether a quote uses in-place, projected, or adjusted income. Try the cap-rate calculator .

### What is a good cap rate for industrial property?

No single cap rate is “good.” It depends on rates, location, building quality, lease term, tenant credit, market rent, and capital needs. A low rate with a strong tenant and long lease may be better than a high rate with near-term vacancy. Compare similar sales and current borrowing costs.

### How is an industrial property valued?

Appraisers and buyers use three approaches: income (capitalized or discounted NOI), usually best for leased investments; sales comparison, often best for owner-user properties; and cost (land plus depreciated replacement cost) as a check. See how buyers underwrite .

### What is net operating income (NOI)?

NOI is rental and other property income minus operating expenses (taxes, insurance, repairs, utilities, and management), before debt service, depreciation, income taxes, and usually capital reserves. Net-lease reimbursements mean NOI is near base rent less unrecovered costs. See NOI .

### How useful is price per square foot for industrial property?

Price per square foot helps compare owner-user and vacant buildings but hides differences in land, clear height, office, yard, condition, and lease terms. Use it with income value and replacement cost, comparing similar buildings in the same submarket and size range.

### What is WALT, and why does it matter?

WALT is remaining lease term weighted by rent or square footage. Longer WALT supports predictable income and financing; shorter WALT adds rollover risk but may let rents reset to market. See WALT .

### What are DSCR and LTV?

DSCR (debt service coverage ratio) divides NOI by annual loan payments; lenders commonly require above 1.0, often 1.25 or higher. LTV (loan-to-value) divides loan amount by property value. The lower loan allowed by these tests usually controls. See DSCR and LTV .

### What are IRR, equity multiple, and cash-on-cash return?

Cash-on-cash is annual pre-tax cash flow divided by equity invested. Equity multiple is total cash returned divided by equity over the hold. IRR annualizes returns based on the timing of all cash flows, including sale proceeds. Each measures something different. See IRR .

### How do you determine market rent for an industrial building?

Market rent comes from signed leases for comparable space (size, location, clear height, doors, office, and condition), adjusted for free rent and improvement allowances. Asking rents show expectations, not deals. Ask brokers or appraisers for lease comparables.

### How do interest rates affect industrial property values?

Higher rates raise borrowing costs and required returns, tending to raise cap rates and lower prices unless rent growth offsets them. Lower rates generally reverse this. Effects are not one-for-one; rent growth, supply and investor demand also matter. Model realistic financing, not the lowest available rate.

## Selling an industrial property

### How do I sell an industrial building?

Obtain a broker opinion and organize leases and financials. Choose broad or targeted marketing, review offers, select a buyer through an LOI, negotiate the purchase agreement, support diligence and close. The selling guide explains.

### How long does it take to sell an industrial property?

A sale typically takes several months for preparation, marketing, offers, negotiation, diligence (often 30 to 60 days), and closing. Environmental findings, financing, estoppels, title, or 1031 timing can extend it. Organize documents before marketing. See the sale process .

### How do I find out what my industrial building is worth?

Request a broker opinion using comparable sales, leases, and buyer demand, or commission an appraisal for a lender, estate, or partnership. Provide the rent roll, leases, expenses, tax bills, and building details. See pricing .

### What documents do I need to sell an industrial property?

Gather leases and amendments, rent roll, two to three years of operating statements, tax bills and appeal history, service contracts, title policy, survey, environmental and condition reports, permits and occupancy certificates, warranties, utility information, and site plans. See preparing documents .

### Is it better to sell an industrial building vacant or leased?

Vacant buildings may attract owner-users willing to pay a premium for the right location and function; leased buildings attract income buyers. Long, market-rate leases often command stronger investor pricing. Short or below-market leases can hurt both buyer pools.

### What does an industrial investment sales broker do?

A sales broker prices and markets property, qualifies buyers, manages tours, confidentiality and offers, negotiates, and coordinates diligence and closing. Sellers usually pay a percentage commission at closing under the listing agreement. Choose recent submarket experience.

### Should I sell off-market or with a full marketing process?

Broad marketing reaches more buyers and may produce a stronger price. Off-market offers privacy, less tenant disruption, and speed, but can leave money on the table. A short list of qualified buyers is a middle path. See confidentiality and marketing .

### What taxes apply when I sell an industrial building?

Federal capital gains tax generally applies to the gain, and depreciation taken is recaptured. For real property, unrecaptured Section 1250 gain is taxed at a federal rate of up to 25 percent. Illinois income tax and, in some cases, the net investment income tax may also apply, and state, county, and local transfer taxes are due at closing. A 1031 exchange can defer gain. Plan with a tax advisor before you list.

### What happens after I accept an offer on my industrial property?

The buyer signs the purchase agreement, deposits earnest money and reviews inspections, environmental, title, survey, leases and estoppels. After diligence, the deposit typically becomes non-refundable except under specified conditions; financing and closing follow. See PSA and earnest money .

### How do I prepare my industrial building for sale?

Organize documents, resolve deferred maintenance that buyers will price aggressively (roof leaks, dock equipment, pavement, life safety), clean up the yard, confirm permits and zoning compliance, address known environmental questions, and line up tenant renewals where possible. See physical preparation .

## Due diligence and environmental

### What is due diligence when buying an industrial property?

Before committing to close, buyers review leases, income, condition, environmental history, title, survey, zoning, permits, utilities, taxes and insurance. Findings support proceeding, renegotiating or walking away. See the due diligence guide .

### What is a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment?

A Phase I ESA reviews records, inspects the site, and interviews relevant parties to identify recognized environmental conditions. Performed under ASTM E1527-21 to satisfy EPA’s All Appropriate Inquiries rule, it may help buyers qualify for certain CERCLA protections. It does not sample soil or groundwater. See environmental diligence .

### How long is a Phase I ESA good for?

All Appropriate Inquiries generally requires key Phase I components completed or updated within 180 days before acquisition; reports over one year old generally need a new assessment. Lenders may impose their own requirements. Match timing to closing.

### What is a Phase II environmental assessment?

A Phase II samples soil, groundwater, vapor, or building materials to test suspected contamination flagged in a Phase I. It is common at sites with historic manufacturing, tanks, dry cleaning, or chemical use. Results may lead to remediation, price changes, insurance, or withdrawal.

### What are common environmental issues at industrial sites?

Frequent issues include leaking underground or aboveground storage tanks, chlorinated solvents from degreasing, petroleum, metals, PCBs in older equipment, asbestos and lead in building materials, vapor intrusion, fill material of unknown origin, and emerging contaminants such as PFAS. Adjacent properties can also contaminate a site through groundwater.

### What is a property condition assessment?

An engineer reviews roof, structure, paving, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, fire protection and accessibility, estimating repair costs and a replacement schedule. Industrial priorities include roof age, docks, slab, sprinklers and truck-court pavement. See physical diligence .

### What is an ALTA survey, and why do lenders want one?

An ALTA/NSPS survey maps boundaries, easements, encroachments, improvements, access, and flood zone to national standards, helping a title insurer remove the standard survey exception. Lenders typically require one. It can confirm truck access, parking, rail spurs, and property-line conflicts. See ALTA survey .

### What does a title commitment show, and what does title insurance cover?

A title commitment lists the owner, legal description, liens, easements, restrictions, and closing requirements. Title insurance covers certain non-excluded defects, such as forged documents or undisclosed liens. Review each exception; easements and restrictions can limit site use. See title commitment .

### What is a tenant estoppel certificate?

A tenant signs an estoppel confirming rent, term, deposits, options, amendments and either party's defaults. Buyers and lenders use it to verify the seller's lease representations. See estoppel certificate .

### What is an Illinois No Further Remediation (NFR) letter?

Illinois EPA typically issues NFR letters through its Site Remediation or leaking UST program after cleanup objectives are met for a defined use. Land-use restrictions or engineered barriers often require maintenance and recording. Read conditions; “clean” does not mean suitable for every use.

## Illinois zoning and property taxes

### What zoning does a warehouse or industrial use need?

Industrial uses generally need manufacturing or industrial zoning. Municipalities define permitted, special and prohibited uses; outdoor storage, truck terminals and heavy manufacturing are often restricted. County zoning applies in unincorporated areas. Obtain the designation and written use confirmation from the local authority.

### What is a Planned Manufacturing District (PMD) in Chicago?

Chicago PMD zoning protects industrial business concentrations from residential and other non-industrial conversion by restricting incompatible uses. Check the City zoning map for boundaries and permissions. See the Chicago research guide .

### What are Chicago’s industrial corridors?

City-designated industrial concentrations guide Chicago land-use policy and economic-development programs. Some corridors have been reviewed or modernized for broader mixed uses. Confirm current designations and zoning with City planning and zoning departments.

### What is the difference between a special use and a variance?

A special or conditional use is allowed after public review, often with conditions. A variance grants relief from a standard such as setback, parking, or height when strict application creates hardship. Both require applications and hearings, so allow time. See special use and variance .

### What is different about industrial property in unincorporated areas?

County rules govern zoning, permits, and often utilities and police outside municipal boundaries. Rules and costs may differ from a neighboring village, and annexation can change them. Confirm jurisdiction and utilities. See unincorporated vs. incorporated .

### How are industrial property taxes calculated in Illinois?

The assessor estimates market value and applies an assessment level; a state or county equalization factor may follow. After exemptions, multiply assessed value by the combined rates of local taxing districts, whose levies set the rates. See the property tax guide .

### Why are Cook County industrial property taxes different from the collar counties?

Cook County assesses industrial property at 25 percent of market value, reassesses by region every three years, and applies a state equalizer. Other counties generally use one-third of market value, township assessors, and annual equalization. District tax rates also differ. See Cook vs. collar counties .

### What is the Cook County Class 6b incentive?

Class 6b lowers assessments for qualifying new, substantially rehabilitated, or reoccupied industrial property. The level is commonly 10 percent of market value for ten years, then 15 and 20 percent in the final two years, versus 25 percent standard. Municipal support and timely application are required. Confirm current rules with the Cook County Assessor. See Cook County incentives .

### How do I appeal industrial property taxes in Illinois?

In Cook County, appeal to the Assessor during the township window, then the Board of Review; elsewhere, appeal to the county Board of Review. Further appeals may go to the state Property Tax Appeal Board or circuit court. Deadlines are short; income, comparable sales, vacancy, or appraisal evidence matters. See appeals and deadlines .

### Who pays real estate transfer tax in Illinois?

Illinois and county transfer taxes usually fall on sellers by custom. Some municipalities add taxes under local ordinances; Chicago's falls largely on buyers. Confirm rates, exemptions and responsibility with your attorney and municipality. See transfer tax .

## The Chicago industrial market

### Why is Chicago a major industrial and logistics hub?

Chicago connects all six Class I railroads and major interstates I-55, I-57, I-80, I-88, I-90, and I-94. O’Hare is a major air-cargo airport, and the region’s workforce and central location put much of the U.S. within one or two days by truck. See the logistics corridors guide .

### How big is the Chicago industrial market?

Chicagoland is among North America’s largest industrial markets, with more than a billion square feet in most brokerage counts. Definitions of area, building size, and property type vary, so compare like-for-like reports.

### What are the main industrial submarkets in Chicagoland?

Reports commonly divide the region into O’Hare, Chicago, I-55, I-80/Joliet, I-88, North and Northwest suburbs and Lake County, South and Southwest suburbs, Fox Valley, southeast Wisconsin, and northwest Indiana. Boundaries vary by firm. See Chicagoland submarkets and corridors .

### What are the I-55 and I-80 industrial corridors?

I-55 runs southwest through Bolingbrook and Romeoville toward Joliet; I-80 crosses Will County around Joliet, New Lenox, and Minooka. Nearby intermodal terminals anchor much of the region’s modern distribution space. See the freight corridor table .

### Why is the O’Hare area important for industrial real estate?

Elk Grove Village, Franklin Park, Bensenville, Wood Dale, and Des Plaines combine O’Hare cargo, interstate and rail access, and older small- and mid-size buildings near the city. Limited land makes it an infill market where functional locations tend to stay leased.

### What intermodal terminals serve Chicagoland?

Class I railroads operate intermodal terminals across Chicagoland. Will County’s BNSF Logistics Park Chicago in Elwood and Union Pacific’s Joliet terminal anchor the I-55/I-80 market, alongside CenterPoint Intermodal Center. See the corridors guide .

### What is the industrial vacancy rate in Chicago?

Chicago’s industrial vacancy changes quarterly by submarket, size, and age; large distribution and small infill buildings can trend differently. Compare current brokerage reports using consistent definitions. The home page links recent news.

### Are Chicago industrial rents going up?

Chicago rents rose with demand over recent years, but growth varies by submarket and new supply. Small-bay and infill rents may differ from big-box rents. Use recent signed comparables for your submarket and size range, not regional averages.

### Which Chicagoland county is best for industrial property?

It depends on use. Cook offers infill access, labor, and O’Hare, but higher taxes; Will has intermodal access and modern buildings; DuPage and Lake have established parks; Kane, McHenry, Kendall, DeKalb, and Grundy offer more land and growth corridors. The nine-county guide links assessor and planning contacts.

### How do I find industrial property for sale in Chicagoland?

Check commercial listings; many small and mid-size buildings trade through brokers or off-market. Set size, county, clear height, door, yard and lease criteria with an industrial investment sales broker. Pavlo Rospopa focuses on 10,000 to 100,000 SF assets across nine Illinois counties; connect on LinkedIn .

## About these questions

Questions reflect common searches, client conversations and recurring industry themes; original answers educate about Chicagoland industrial real estate. See the industrial investor Q&A and glossary for investor topics and definitions.

Investor Q&A · 10,000 to 100,000 SF industrial

# What experienced industrial investors ask, and how to think about the answers

Educational answers, not advice on any specific property, loan, tax position, or investment.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Experienced buyers ask these questions about small and midsize industrial buildings in deal conversations, investor forums and conference panels. The questions are theirs; Pavlo Rospopa's answers provide general Chicagoland education.

- Price off documented income, then test the hold with explicit rollover, capital, and exit assumptions. Cap rate and IRR answer different questions.
- Buy for likely tenants: small-bay and bulk distribution needs differ.
- Underwrite Illinois taxes after sale, not the seller's bill; never assume incentives transfer.
- Most “surprises” are knowable in diligence: roof, pavement, fire protection, environmental history, zoning conformity, and lease clauses.
- Sell, refinance, or hold is a capital question first and a market-timing question second.
- Owner lens: Stress correlated setbacks together, such as tenant loss, tax or insurance increases, a major repair, and tighter refinancing, rather than testing each downside in isolation.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_Industrial buildings in Elk Grove Village, Illinois. Review tenant exposure, lease rollover, capital requirements and financing together._

## Pricing and returns

### Is cap rate or IRR the right way to price a 10,000 to 100,000 SF building?

Cap rate divides documented NOI by price on a stated basis. IRR models income through lease expirations, capital spending, financing and sale. They answer different questions.

Short leases, few tenants, and above- or below-market rents can make a small building’s in-place cap misleading. Price from documented income, then model each lease, including downtime, improvements, commissions, and a defensible exit cap. Try the investment guide’s cap-rate calculator .

### How much weight should replacement cost carry?

Replacement cost (land, construction, soft costs, and lease-up) frames downside. Buying well below build cost limits new competition at your rent level, but cost does not set value: low clear height or a cramped truck court can make a building worth less than “cost.”

Use replacement cost to check price per square foot and expected competing supply, not as a target. See building types and specifications for fixable and permanent features.

### What does “below-market rent” really mean, and how do I underwrite the mark-to-market?

Only signed comparable leases establish market rent. For small-bay space, suite size, office finish, doors, power, and yard rights narrow the comparison; asking rents are not signed deals.

Rent resets at lease expiration, so model retention probability, downtime, improvements, commissions, and free rent for each expiration. Do not pay for the upside in the price and count it again in the pro forma.

### How should I set the exit cap rate and hold period?

Exit cap rate is often the most sensitive assumption; the building will be older at sale. A lower exit than entry cap needs justification, such as a longer lease or completed renovation.

Test a higher exit cap, lower market rent, longer downtime, and delayed sale. If the deal only works in the base case, that case is doing too much work.

## Building and functionality

### Does clear height matter for buildings this size, or only for bulk distribution?

In 10,000 to 40,000 SF spaces, service companies, contractors, light assembly and last-mile operators may favor drive-in doors, power, office ratio, parking and yard over extra clearance. Distribution and third-party logistics tenants prioritize docks, truck court and racking height.

Buy and underwrite for likely tenants. The building-fit checklist covers tour measurements.

### What makes a Class B or C building “functionally obsolete,” and can capital fix it?

Capital can fix roofs, lighting, dock equipment, pavement, offices, electrical service, and sometimes add dock positions. It cannot fix low clear height, tight columns, a shallow truck court, high site coverage without expansion land, or poor access. Those limits cap rent and narrow the buyer pool.

Price permanent limitations. A well-located, functional Class B building can still be durable if it serves local demand and is hard to replace.

### How do I value excess land or an outdoor storage yard attached to a building?

Confirm zoning and approvals for outdoor storage, trailer parking or equipment staging. Verify access, surfacing, lighting, drainage, stormwater compliance and separate leaseability. Even industrial districts may restrict yard use.

Permitted, separately leasable yard is worth more than yard that is merely tolerated. The nine-county hub links zoning authorities.

### Multi-tenant or single-tenant: which is less risky in this size range?

Multi-tenant buildings spread vacancy risk but bring more frequent rollover, demising, metering, and management. Single-tenant buildings are simpler to own and finance but carry binary vacancy risk tied to one company.

Choose the risk you can manage. If you cannot lease small suites efficiently, diversification on paper becomes vacancy in practice.

## Tenants and leases

### How do I underwrite tenant credit when the tenants are private companies?

Request what the lease allows: financial statements, payment history, time in business, ownership, guaranties, and security. Also assess durability: heavy equipment, permits, customer proximity, and specialized build-outs make moving costly.

In small-bay buildings, re-leasing ease may matter more than one tenant’s credit. A functional suite in a liquid submarket is its own credit support.

### Which lease clauses most affect value?

- Expense pass-throughs , especially whether real estate taxes after a reassessment are recoverable and whether CAM is capped.
- Roof, structure, HVAC, and pavement obligations: who replaces, not just who repairs.
- Renewal options at fixed or capped rents , which can cap your mark-to-market.
- Termination, contraction, assignment, and sublease rights .
- Hazardous materials, outdoor storage, trailer parking, and hours clauses that govern how the property may actually be used.
- Holdover, security, and guaranty terms.

Confirm all of it with tenant estoppels before closing. The lease-review checklist covers the mechanics.

### How do I underwrite rollover and downtime realistically?

Model each lease expiration instead of using a blended vacancy factor. Assign retention probability, downtime, improvement and commission costs, and free rent; then test simultaneous departures, lower renewal rent, and longer lease-up.

For concentrated rollover, consider negotiating early renewals or extensions. Sellers may also value certainty.

### In a sale-leaseback, what am I really buying?

The seller-tenant’s ability to pay during the lease and the real estate if it stops. Rent may reflect the seller’s financing need, not the market; compare it with market rent to assess residual risk.

Weigh lease term, guaranties, reporting covenants, and maintenance alongside price. The selling guide explains the owner-user’s perspective.

## Diligence and risk

### When is a Phase I enough, and when do I need a Phase II?

Phase I identifies recognized environmental conditions through records, interviews and a site visit, without sampling. Phase II samples soil, groundwater or vapor when Phase I, site history or surrounding uses indicate risk. Lenders frequently require it for flagged conditions.

Allow time for sampling and lab work. Understand the Illinois EPA Site Remediation Program and no-further-remediation letters before relying on them. The due diligence guide covers the process; EPA’s All Appropriate Inquiries page explains the federal framework.

### Which physical items most often become price adjustments?

Roof age and warranty, pavement and truck court, dock equipment, office HVAC, and electrical capacity. For storage users, confirm sprinkler adequacy for the next tenant’s commodities and rack heights; upgrades can be expensive.

A property condition assessment schedules these costs and supports negotiations.

### If the building is already operating, how much does zoning conformity matter?

It matters for changes of use, expansion, outdoor storage or different tenants. A legal nonconforming use may continue but not expand or restart after a lapse. Obtain the zoning designation and written municipal confirmation of planned uses.

### What should I know about flood and stormwater for Chicago-area industrial sites?

Check the FEMA flood map first, then the local stormwater rules: in Cook County the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District administers a watershed management ordinance, and the collar counties and municipalities have their own requirements. Detention obligations can affect expansion plans and yard surfacing, and a flat, paved industrial site is not immune to drainage problems.

## Illinois taxes and incentives

### Will my purchase trigger a reassessment, and how do I underwrite it?

A recorded Illinois sale can inform assessed value. Cook County reassesses by region every three years; collar counties use their own cycles with annual equalization. Underwrite your likely post-sale tax bill, not the seller’s, and confirm leases allow recovery of increases.

Build an appeal calendar during diligence. The property tax guide links all nine county assessment offices.

### Does a Cook County Class 6b incentive stay with the property when it sells?

Do not assume transfer. Check current Cook County Assessor bulletins for remaining reduced assessments, ownership or occupancy change requirements, renewal resolutions and termination conditions. Underwrite with and without the incentive; treat the difference as negotiable risk.

### How does a TIF district affect an industrial owner?

You pay taxes normally; TIF redirects the increment above a base to public purposes, often under redevelopment agreements. Check binding property agreements, district expiration and dependent incentives in governing documents, not the map legend.

## Debt and capital

### How do lenders size loans on small industrial buildings, and what trips borrowers up?

Lenders test loan-to-value, debt service coverage, and often debt yield using their own income and expense definitions. Common hurdles include leases shorter than the loan (requiring rollover reserves or structure), environmental findings, appraisal gaps, recourse, and prepayment limits.

Confirm definitions early and model the lender’s case. The debt-service calculator shows the arithmetic.

### How should I think about refinancing risk at loan maturity?

Test whether the property still carries itself with a higher rate, lower loan amount, and tougher appraisal. Usual defenses include moderate leverage, staggered maturities, extension options, and a capital plan independent of cash-out proceeds.

### When does SBA 504 financing matter to an investor?

Owner-users compete for the same buildings. A company occupying most of a building can often use the SBA 504 program 's long-term fixed-rate component to justify a price beyond rental income value. Expect this competition for vacant or soon-vacant buildings, not long-leased investments.

## Timing, exit, and sourcing

### How do I decide between selling, refinancing, and holding?

Start with upcoming rollover, roof or pavement costs, loan maturity, tax basis, an exchange plan, and liquidity. Then ask whether you would buy the building today at its potential sale price. If not, reconsider the hold.

The selling guide covers buyer questions and the sale process.

### Who is the likely buyer of my building at exit?

For 10,000 to 100,000 SF buildings, likely buyers include owner-users, private investors, exchange buyers, and smaller funds. Size, condition, and leases shape the pool: vacant functional buildings attract owner-users; leased buildings with term attract investors and exchange buyers. Prepare the document file for likely buyers.

### How are off-market deals really sourced?

Through owner outreach, broker networks, estates or partnerships in transition, and lease expirations. Be fundable and ready, but remember “off-market” can mean mispriced either way. Underwrite it like any other deal.

## Where these questions come from

Questions paraphrase investor forum, conference, lender and negotiation themes, not individual posts or comments. These general educational answers concern 10,000 to 100,000 SF Chicagoland industrial properties. Apply them with your advisers.

Send a question on LinkedIn . For broader topics, see the industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions .

## Building fit and insurance

### How should a small-bay owner choose suite sizes?

I would really recommend changing the approach from "if you build it they will come" to "who do I want to cater to and what do they need".

Joseph Gozlan on BiggerPockets · Dec 2022

The smaller space markets are very local in nature,

Mark Duclos in SIOR Pulse · Jun 2023 · Interview focused on Connecticut and western Massachusetts

In square footage, the pipeline is concentrated in megabuildings, which have seen the most decline in demand,

Lisa DeNight in NAIOP Development magazine · Winter 2023/24 · Historical national industrial outlook, not a small-bay forecast

Pavlo's take

Pavlo starts with the intended use, access, loading, power and permitted occupancy. Tenant interviews and local leasing evidence are more useful than a universal ideal bay size; test the proposed layout and approvals before building.

Read the guide: Industrial building types and specifications .

### Why do contractor-yard rents differ?

Maybe look into why they vary so much, maybe some are offering more amenities, better security, better access, nicer property.

Grant Rothenburger on BiggerPockets · Aug 2018

Pavlo's take

Pavlo verifies outdoor-storage permission, lease rights, surface, drainage, security and actual truck paths. Two yards with similar area may support very different operations; a quoted rent does not establish usable access.

Read the guide: Truck access, swept paths and offtracking .

### How should an owner compare insurance quotes?

The best policy (considering price and coverage) will vary by location, construction, loss history, use of property, etc.

John Mocker on BiggerPockets · Dec 2020

Policy exclusions or limitations can create compliance issues and unexpected gaps at renewal or claim time,

Matt Dvorak in Northmarq · Apr 2026 · Insurance interview

Lenders are placing greater emphasis on obtaining complete copies of insurance policies rather than relying on ACORD certificates, which are now seen as less dependable documentation,

Whitney Ronning in Northmarq · Apr 2026 · Lender-compliance perspective

Pavlo's take

Pavlo recommends comparable limits, valuation, exclusions and deductibles, reviewed with a licensed commercial insurance adviser. Update occupancy and building information before renewal; a cheaper quote may remove protection rather than reduce the same risk.

Read the guide: Commercial insurance coverage and renewal review .

## Cook County taxes

### Who can help review a Cook County tax appeal?

You are most definitely looking for a property tax attorney

Aaron Zimmerman on BiggerPockets · Nov 2025

Commercial property assessments are calculated by determining a property’s use, estimated income, market-level vacancy, collections loss, and expenses.

## Refinancing

### How should an owner plan for a balloon payment?

Of course tides and environments can change drastically between " re financing" which is causing a lot of concern now, especially for retail

Will G. on BiggerPockets · Oct 2017

From an equity investor’s perspective, you’re willing to take a risk if you think that there is a potential big payout. If you’re a lender, there is no upside besides getting paid back.

Jamie Woodwell in NAIOP Development magazine · Winter 2023/24 · Historical discussion of office lending and credit risk

## Renewing versus re-leasing

### Should an owner hold out for a higher renewal rent?

The landlord doesn't want you to to leave but only to the extent that finding a new tenant costs more than the discount against the current market price they'd have to give you to stay.

AnthonyMouse on Hacker News · Jun 2026 · Forum comment about commercial vacancy

And because the pond is more shallow, landlords, while still in the drivers’ seat, cannot push rates up like they used to.

Mark Duclos in SIOR Pulse · Jun 2023 · Historical Hartford warehouse leasing discussion

Pavlo compares the renewal with a documented re-leasing scenario: downtime, carrying costs, tenant improvements, commissions and tenant credit. Neither a forum view nor an older regional interview establishes today's achievable rent; use current local evidence and test the cash-flow trade-off.

Industrial guide · Building function and specifications

# Industrial building types and specifications

Educational, not an engineering report or valuation.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Industrial building types and specifications for buyers, tenants, lenders and advisers reviewing 10,000 to 100,000 square foot Chicagoland assets.

- Loading, clear height, power, truck movement, fire protection, and zoning determine utility, not the building label.
- Fit depends on operations, storage, labor, and equipment; a building suited to one user may not suit another.
- Class A, B, and C are informal labels. Tie them to verifiable features.
- Confirm specifications through documents, measurements, municipal records, and qualified professionals.
- A clear seller spec sheet can reduce re-trading and reach the right buyer or tenant pool.
- Owner lens: Prioritize costly-to-change features such as clear height, column grid, truck court, power, fire protection, and legal yard use over cosmetic fit-out when weighing long-term adaptability.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_Warehouse racking, columns and lighting illustrate physical features that affect operations. Verify dimensions and specifications for the property being evaluated._

## Why type and spec matter for 10,000 to 100,000 SF buildings

Owner-users and private investors buy 10,000 to 100,000 square feet; tenants are often local or regional. One building can serve operations, rental income or re-tenanting.

Owner-users assess doors, power, production flow, office area, parking, and expansion room. Tenants compare occupancy cost, timing, lease obligations, and operational disruption. Investors review the lease and potential replacement users.

The industrial building evaluation checklist and seller guide focus on function, records, and verifiable facts.

- Function: Does the building support the use without unusual workarounds?
- Flexibility: Could another user occupy it if the first plan changes?
- Risk: Are there physical, zoning, environmental, or utility constraints that affect timing or cost?

## Common industrial building types

Verify physical features, permitted use and operating history; type labels do not replace diligence.

**Industrial building types and what to verify**
- Type: Typical operations: Defining features: What to verify
- Bulk warehouse or distribution: Storage, fulfillment, wholesale distribution, and regional goods movement.: Open warehouse, multiple dock-high positions, trailer circulation, and racking potential.: Clear height , docks, truck court, fire protection, trailer parking, and racking layout.
- Light industrial or small-bay: Service trades, last-mile operations, small distribution, contractor storage, and local businesses.: Divisible suites, drive-in doors, modest office finish, shared parking or yard.: Demising, utility metering, parking allocation, overhead doors, lease terms, and permitted uses.
- Manufacturing: Production, assembly, fabrication, packaging, and repair. Heavy manufacturing typically needs more equipment, utilities, ventilation, or process capacity than light manufacturing.: Power, slab capacity, clear spans, ventilation, cranes, process piping, and office/production separation.: Electrical service, floor loads, air permits, hazardous materials, equipment anchoring, drains, and zoning.
- Flex or office-warehouse: Showroom, research, light assembly, service, office support, and warehouse storage.: Higher office share, customer entry, flexible warehouse, and mixed parking/loading.: Office quality, HVAC zoning, parking, ceiling height, loading, and economical office reuse.
- Cold storage or food-grade: Refrigerated or frozen storage, food handling, beverage, pharmaceutical, and temperature-sensitive distribution.: Insulated envelope, refrigeration, drains, washable surfaces, dock seals, and temperature controls.: Temperature zones, equipment age, sanitary design, backup power, permits, roof penetrations, and operating costs.
- Truck terminal or cross-dock: Freight transfer, route consolidation, parcel handling, and short-dwell movement.: Opposing or numerous doors, shallow storage, paved areas, and trailer circulation.: Cross-dock layout, door spacing, pavement, access, lighting, security, and operating hours.
- Industrial outdoor storage or yard: Fleet, contractor, equipment, container, material, and trailer storage.: Usable fenced land, stable surface, security, drainage, and limited building area.: Zoning, special-use approvals, surface, stormwater, screening, lighting, and neighbor constraints.
- Rail-served industrial: Bulk materials, manufacturing inputs, transload, plastics, metals, paper, lumber, and heavy commodities.: Rail spur or siding, loading, interior or exterior rail access, and railroad/operator agreements.: Active service, track condition, switch rights, clearance, commodity limits, easements, and maintenance.
- Data or specialty industrial: Data, lab, clean manufacturing, life-safety, fleet electrification, and other specialized uses.: Unusual power, cooling, redundancy, security, floor loads, or regulatory needs.: Utility commitments, cooling, code, specialty permits, removal obligations, and improvement reuse value.

## Specifications explained and why each matters

Explain each specification's practical effect and separate measured facts from assumptions or broker shorthand.

- **Clear height**: Clear height is usually measured from the finished floor to the lowest obstruction, not the roof deck. It affects racking, equipment, lighting, and sprinklers; check beams, joists, ducts, heaters, fans, and piping.
- **Column spacing and speed bays**: Spacing affects storage, forklift movement, production cells, and demising. Speed bays can add dock staging depth; verify dimensions and obstructions.
- **Dock-high doors and door ratio**: Dock-high loading supports trailer-height movement, often critical for distribution. Door-to-area ratios compare loading intensity, but the right ratio depends on operations, trailer dwell, staffing, and scheduling.
- **Drive-in doors**: These admit vehicles, equipment, or vans at grade. Verify clear opening, apron slope, condition, security, and safe use across grade changes.
- **Dock levelers, seals, shelters, and bumpers**: These affect safety, weather protection, handling, and efficiency. Review condition, capacity, controls, and maintenance records.
- **Truck court depth and turning**: Circulation depends on court depth, trailer length, door angle, opposing parking, curbs, fences, and stored materials. Test the site plan against the intended truck using the truck dimensions and turning-path reference to distinguish body, cargo, and overall dimensions and prepare a fleet-specific swept-path review.
- **Trailer and car parking**: Trailer, car, fleet, and visitor spaces serve different functions. Verify striping, easements, shared rights, zoning, and outdoor-storage permissions.
- **Slab thickness, flatness, and load**: Slab performance affects racking, forklifts, equipment, and high-bay storage. Relevant ACI and ASTM concepts do not replace a structural engineer's review of thickness, joints, flatness, condition, and material load capacity.
- **Power**: Record amps, voltage, phase, panels, switchgear, transformer location, spare capacity, and utility service. Three-phase power often matters for machinery, compressors, welders, refrigeration, charging, and process loads.
- **Lighting**: Lighting affects safety, productivity, and energy cost. Check fixture type, controls, exterior and emergency lighting, and measured levels where needed.
- **Fire protection**: Wet-pipe systems, ESFR sprinklers , in-rack sprinklers, pumps, and alarms support different storage designs. A fire-protection engineer and the authority having jurisdiction should review commodity, storage height, rack layout, and NFPA 13 .
- **Roof**: Type, age, warranty, drainage, penetrations, insulation, and repair history inform capital planning. A roof consultant can distinguish maintenance from near-term replacement risk.
- **HVAC, ventilation, and warehouse heat**: Industrial HVAC often varies across office, production, and warehouse areas. Check heaters, make-up air, exhaust, ventilation, cooling, controls, and proposed-use code requirements.
- **Office finish percentage**: Office area may suit administrative users but reduce warehouse depth. Confirm rentable area, quality, HVAC, restrooms, demising walls, and conversion cost.
- **Floor-to-floor height for mezzanines**: Mezzanines and two-level offices depend on clearances, structure, stairs, egress, accessibility, and fire protection. Verify permits, load rating, and inclusion in reported square footage.
- **Site coverage and expansion land**: Low site coverage may leave room for yard, parking, or expansion, but zoning, setbacks, stormwater, utilities, easements, and wetlands can constrain use. Vacant land is not necessarily buildable.
- **Zoning and permitted use**: Zoning controls uses, outdoor storage, parking, signage, truck traffic, hours, and nonconforming rights. Confirm the intended use with the municipality, not just the district name.

For safety and workplace requirements, start with applicable code officials and qualified professionals; federal OSHA materials may also be relevant to operations.

## Class A, B, and C as informal labels

Class labels are market shorthand, not an official standard. Tie them to inspectable, documented facts.

**Informal ways people describe industrial building class**
- Label: Common description: Caution
- Class A: Newer or recently modernized building with stronger loading, height, systems, truck circulation, life-safety features, and institutional-quality records.: A small Class A building may still be wrong for a user if doors, power, or zoning do not fit.
- Class B: Functional building with some older features, moderate office finish, usable loading, and a condition profile that may require selective capital work.: Class B can be a broad category, so list the actual strengths and weaknesses.
- Class C: Older or more specialized building with lower clear height, limited loading, heavier deferred maintenance, or narrower reuse.: Class C does not mean unusable; it means the buyer pool may be more specific and diligence may be more important.

## How specs translate to buyer and tenant pools

Specifications determine who can operate efficiently. Strong doors, turning, power, and fire protection may broaden distribution or manufacturing demand compared with a similarly sized building with limited utility.

Functional obsolescence is a mismatch with current operating needs, such as low clear height, shallow truck courts, insufficient power, limited parking, excess office finish, difficult column spacing, or loading unsuited to building size.

Investors assess re-tenanting risk by estimating the potential user pool, improvement timing, and required capital. See the investment diligence guide and commercial leasing guide .

- Broader pool: flexible layout, adequate power, code-compliant improvements, documented systems, and common loading patterns.
- Narrower pool: very specialized equipment, unusual floor plan, unresolved environmental history, nonconforming yard, or limited truck access.
- Seller takeaway: disclose constraints clearly and support strengths with records rather than adjectives.

## Spec sheet checklist

A spec sheet helps buyers, tenants, lenders and inspectors verify facts. Flag unknowns; do not guess.

**Items to include in an industrial property spec sheet**
- Item: Where to verify: Who verifies
- Building and land area: Survey, assessor records, appraisal, plans, leases, and measurement reports.: Surveyor, architect, appraiser, broker, or buyer representative.
- Clear height: Field measurement to lowest obstruction and building plans if available.: Broker, tenant, architect, engineer, or racking consultant.
- Column spacing: Plans, field measurement, and racking layout.: Architect, engineer, racking vendor, or tenant operations team.
- Dock and drive-in doors: Site tour, door schedule, dock equipment records, and photographs.: Broker, property manager, dock contractor, or inspector.
- Truck court and turning: ALTA survey, site plan, truck-turn exhibit, and field observation.: Civil engineer, surveyor, buyer, or logistics consultant.
- Parking and trailer storage: Striping plan, zoning file, lease rights, easements, and field count.: Broker, municipality, surveyor, or land-use attorney.
- Power service: Utility records, electrical one-line, panels, transformer, and electrician inspection.: Electrical contractor, engineer, utility, or tenant equipment vendor.
- Fire protection: Sprinkler drawings, inspection reports, hydraulic calculations, and alarm records.: Fire-protection contractor, engineer, insurer, and authority having jurisdiction.
- Roof: Warranty, roof plan, maintenance invoices, leak log, and roof report.: Roof consultant, contractor, inspector, or lender consultant.
- Slab: Plans, cores if appropriate, condition survey, and load review.: Structural engineer, concrete consultant, or buyer equipment vendor.
- HVAC and ventilation: Equipment schedules, service records, field inspection, and code review.: Mechanical contractor, engineer, or property condition assessor.
- Zoning and use: Municipal zoning map, zoning letter, permits, and certificates of occupancy.: Municipality, land-use attorney, buyer, or zoning consultant.
- Environmental history: Phase I ESA, permits, tank records, spill records, and owner interviews.: Environmental consultant and counsel.
- Title and survey matters: Title commitment , exception documents, ALTA survey , and recorded easements.: Title company, surveyor, and real estate attorney.

For regional research sources, the county hub links to assessment offices across Cook, DeKalb, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake, McHenry, and Will counties.

> This guide is general education, not engineering, environmental, legal, tax, appraisal, brokerage, or investment advice. Verify measurements, code requirements, zoning, records, environmental matters, and transaction decisions with qualified professionals before acting.

Industrial guide · Fleet and site fit

# Truck dimensions and turning paths

Published and sources checked October 6, 2026 . Metric conversions are rounded.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Use these sourced examples to assess loading, gates, driveways, yards, and truck courts. Cargo capacity, legal road dimensions, and maneuvering space are different measurements.

- A 53-foot trailer is not a 53-foot tractor-trailer combination. A box-truck body size is not the overall truck length.
- A container's dimensions alone do not describe the tractor, chassis, loaded height, or turning envelope.
- There is no universal truck turning radius or safe truck-court depth. Require fleet-specific swept-path review by a qualified engineer.
- Owner lens: A site constraint can narrow future users even when the building itself is functional. Confirm recorded access and easements, gates, staging, and fleet-specific swept paths before valuing yard or loading improvements.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_Vehicle size, staging, and maneuvering space must be reviewed together. Confirm the fleet and swept path against a surveyed site plan._

## Tractors and semitrailers

A tractor alone includes cab and power unit; wheelbase, axles, sleeper and fifth-wheel position vary. A tractor plus semitrailer is articulated; overall length depends on both vehicles and their connection. Do not guess tractor length or treat a trailer label as rig length.

**Semitrailer length references, not overall combination dimensions**
- Reference: Imperial: Metric: What the number means
- 48-foot semitrailer: 48 ft: 14.63 m: FHWA describes the minimum semitrailer length states must allow on the National Network and reasonable access routes, subject to grandfathered provisions. Not interior cargo length.
- 53-foot semitrailer: 53 ft: 16.15 m: FHWA's Illinois grandfathered-length table lists 53 ft. This is the trailer length reference, not an overall rig length or a turning template.

FHWA states there is no federal overall-length limit for tractor-semitrailer combinations on the National Network and reasonable access routes. Its general commercial-vehicle width limit is 102 in (8 ft 6 in; about 2.6 m), subject to exceptions. Neither statement confirms local-road or driveway access. Check current Illinois rules, route restrictions, permits, axle positions, and fleet dimensions.

There is no federal commercial-vehicle height requirement. FHWA describes most state limits as 13 ft 6 in to 14 ft (about 4.11 to 4.27 m), subject to lower clearances and exceptions. This does not authorize a height in Illinois; check the route and current state and local rules.

## Straight and box trucks

A straight truck’s cargo body shares the cab’s chassis. Rental examples below give interior cargo-box dimensions , not exterior bodies, door openings, overall lengths or roof heights.

**Penske published interior dimensions, up to the stated sizes**
- Rental label: Interior L &times; W &times; H, imperial: Interior L &times; W &times; H, metric: Source and limitation
- 16-foot box truck: 16 ft &times; 7 ft 7 in &times; 6 ft 6 in: 4.88 &times; 2.31 &times; 1.98 m: Penske 16-foot truck ; approximate maximum interior dimensions.
- 26-foot box truck: 25 ft 11 in &times; 8 ft 1 in &times; 8 ft 1 in: 7.90 &times; 2.46 &times; 2.46 m: Penske 26-foot truck ; approximate maximum interior dimensions.

Penske says dimensions vary by manufacturer. Neither cited rental page publishes overall external vehicle length. Its commercial light-duty range lists 12- and 16-foot box trucks and 16- and 18-foot cabovers; these labels are not universal specifications.

For a 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, or 26 ft body (about 3.66, 4.27, 4.88, 5.49, 6.10, 6.71, 7.32, or 7.92 m), obtain a model-specific body/chassis drawing. These conversions do not establish availability or interior dimensions. Separately verify overall length, exterior width including protrusions, loaded and unloaded height, wheelbase, rear overhang, door opening, and liftgate deployment.

## Containers and chassis

20- and 40-foot dry containers, including high cubes, are containers alone , not road vehicles. Nominal lengths are not usable interior dimensions. A high cube has a taller body; chassis deck, tires, suspension, and load add height in road transport.

**Maersk dry-container outside-size references, rounded nominal classes**
- Equipment: L &times; W &times; H, published imperial: Approximate metric conversion
- 20-foot standard steel: 20 ft &times; 8 ft &times; 8 ft 6 in: 6.10 &times; 2.44 &times; 2.59 m
- 40-foot standard steel: 40 ft &times; 8 ft &times; 8 ft 6 in: 12.19 &times; 2.44 &times; 2.59 m
- 40-foot high-cube steel: 40 ft &times; 8 ft &times; 9 ft 6 in: 12.19 &times; 2.44 &times; 2.90 m

Source: Maersk dry equipment specifications (PDF, page 1) . These rounded size classes are separate from interior and door-opening dimensions. Metric values convert the nominal sizes; they are not precise ISO dimensions or measurements of a specific unit. They exclude chassis and tractor. Obtain equipment drawings for clearance work.

Request the carrier's drawing for the exact equipment's exterior, interior, and door opening. For a chassis combination, also obtain chassis length, axle positions, container placement, loaded height, and tractor geometry. The container label cannot establish overall height or turning clearance. ISO 668 is the dimensional/classification standard; its full specification is not reproduced here.

## Turning circle, swept path, and offtracking

- **Turning circle diameter vs. radius**: Diameter spans a circle; radius is half only when both use the same circle and measurement convention. A curb-to-curb wheel path is not a wall-to-wall body envelope. Ask which reference point, steering lock, speed, and maneuver were measured.
- **Swept path and outer sweep**: A swept path is the area a vehicle occupies during a maneuver. Its outer boundary includes front corners, mirrors, body overhang, and trailer swing, not just tire tracks.
- **Offtracking**: Rear wheels and a trailer do not follow the tractor's front-wheel path in a low-speed turn; they commonly track inward. Trailer length, wheelbase, axle locations, articulation, steering, and approach angle change the path.
- **Design vehicle**: AASHTO labels such as WB-62 and WB-67 describe specific geometric templates, not interchangeable fleet measurements or a universal radius. A qualified engineer must select a current design vehicle and compare it with the site's fleet and maneuvers.

Cited fleet specifications do not establish a complete configuration’s turning radius, so none is given. Forward circulation, dock backing, opposing traffic and queuing require different checks. FHWA road-size limits are not turning templates.

## Site-review checklist

- Identify the fleet: exact tractor, trailer, straight-truck, or container/chassis configuration, wheelbases, axle positions, body projections, height, and operating loads.
- Survey the constraints: gate openings, curb returns, driveways, dock angles, court depth, grade changes, fences, bollards, poles, parked vehicles, easements, fire access, snow storage, and overhead obstructions.
- Test the maneuver: have a qualified civil/transportation engineer perform fleet-specific swept-path analysis for entry, turns, backing, unloading, and exit, including required operational margins and conflicts.
- Check access and operation: local truck routes, bridge/underpass restrictions, delivery rules, pavement capacity, loading equipment, and municipal approvals. Legal road width or nominal cargo size is not a guaranteed safe clearance.

Also use the building evaluation checklist , building specifications and industrial due-diligence guide .

## Primary sources and limitations

- FHWA: Federal Size Regulations for Commercial Motor Vehicles , including the Illinois semitrailer grandfathered-length table. This explanatory report is not a current local-route approval; actual regulations govern.
- Penske 16-foot truck and Penske 26-foot truck : approximate interior dimensions that vary by manufacturer.
- Penske commercial light-duty trucks : published fleet labels, not overall vehicle drawings.
- ISO 668 catalog : container classification/dimension standard; full tables require access to the standard.
- Maersk dry equipment specifications (PDF) : published nominal outside-size classes for standard and high-cube steel containers, with separate interior and door-opening specifications.
- AASHTO publications : the Green Book contains design-vehicle guidance. Its paid dimensional/turning templates are not reproduced or replaced with guessed values.

> Scope. Educational reference, not engineering, construction, traffic, safety, or legal advice. No table here authorizes a clearance, maneuver, vehicle movement, or site design. Confirm specifications and current requirements with the fleet, carrier, responsible authorities, and qualified engineers.
