Published: 2026-10-02 · Updated: 2026-10-10

Operations & property suitability

# Evaluating Chicago industrial real estate

No current inventory or market statistics are represented.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Compare industrial space against a written checklist of storage, production, loading and staffing needs.

- List storage, production, loading, and staffing needs before touring.
- Verify clear height, loading, truck court, slab, power, and fire protection through measurement and professional review, not listing figures.
- Test routes, truck restrictions, and access; highway or rail proximity does not prove usable freight access.
- Review flood exposure and environmental history; commission transaction-appropriate diligence.
- Owner lens: A building that fits today's operation may be hard to re-lease later. Record the legal use and estimate the cost to adapt it for another plausible user.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_Warehouse interior with selective pallet racking: clear height, column spacing, lighting, and floor condition all affect how a building works._

## Match the actual use, not just the label

- **Warehouse and distribution**: Assess storage layout, throughput, racking, fire protection, dock capacity, and trailer circulation, not just building size.
- **Logistics and last-mile operations**: Test routes to customers, vehicle access, dispatch, parking, and permitted hours. Straight-line distance does not establish delivery time.
- **Manufacturing**: Have qualified specialists review equipment loads, process utilities, ventilation, wastewater, vibration, noise, and required permits.
- **Flex space**: Office and industrial areas may have different physical and code requirements. Confirm permitted activity, buildout scope, and fit for the business.

Record pallet or equipment dimensions, inventory type, peak daily vehicle movements, shifts, and growth assumptions. Special storage or processes may add requirements absent from a generic listing.

## A building-fit checklist

**Items to verify before leasing or purchasing**
- Feature: What to verify
- Clear height and columns: Measure clearance below obstructions, not roof height. Match column spacing to equipment and storage.
- Loading: Check dock-high and drive-in doors, dimensions, condition, equipment, staging, and shared-use restrictions.
- Truck court and yard: Test turning and backing with the actual vehicle. Confirm trailer parking, outdoor-storage permissions, access rights, and snow storage. See fleet-specific swept-path checks ; nominal trailer or body size does not establish clearance.
- Floor and structure: Have qualified professionals assess slab condition, flatness, load capacity, and equipment or rack anchoring.
- Power and utilities: Confirm voltage, phase, service capacity, and availability with utilities and equipment needs. Verify upgrade cost and schedule.
- Fire protection: Confirm the system suits the commodity, packaging, rack design, and storage height.
- Roof and building systems: Review condition, service life, maintenance records, and repair or replacement responsibility.
- People and access: Check employee and visitor parking, accessibility, restrooms, office needs, ventilation, and pedestrian/vehicle separation.

Verify advertised clear height, docks and power through records, measurement and professional review, not inference.

## Research the location as an operating network

Evaluate routes to suppliers, customers, freight facilities and employees. Check truck restrictions, bridge and clearance limits, highway access and operating-hour traffic. Airport, rail or expressway proximity does not prove practical freight access.

The Chicagoland industrial real estate hub links operational questions to official jurisdiction, planning, zoning and parcel sources for Illinois's Cook, DeKalb, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake, McHenry and Will counties. Indiana and Wisconsin are outside scope.

Confirm municipality and county before researching zoning. Review outdoor storage, truck parking, production, and extended hours for the specific property. The commercial property research guide organizes zoning, tax, and building-record checks.

Review flood exposure, drainage, and property history. Commission transaction-appropriate environmental diligence; appearance does not establish that land is uncontaminated.

## Bring these questions to the tour

- What is verified, what is estimated, and what still needs an inspection?
- Can the exact operation be permitted here, including storage and vehicle activity?
- Which improvements are required before occupancy, who pays, and what is the approval schedule?
- Are loading, yard, parking, or utilities shared with other occupants?
- Who maintains and replaces the roof, structure, docks, pavement, and fire-protection system?
- What limits expansion, assignment, subleasing, or later resale?

Use the occupancy-cost and lease checklist for leases or acquisition diligence and financing risk for purchases. Low rent or price may not offset an operational mismatch.

## Official sources for follow-up

- Chicago zoning map and Department of Buildings : city zoning and building research; suburban authorities are separate.
- Chicago Metropolitan Agency for Planning : regional transportation and planning context.
- FEMA Flood Map Service Center : mapped flood hazards.
- EPA: All Appropriate Inquiries : environmental due-diligence background for acquisitions, not a property clearance.

> This is a general evaluation framework, not engineering, fire-code, environmental, or legal advice. Obtain property-specific advice before committing to equipment, construction, a lease, or a purchase.

Industrial guide · Physical and environmental diligence

# Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental

Educational, not legal, environmental, engineering, or investment advice.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Physical, environmental, title, survey, zoning, lease and utility diligence for industrial acquisitions across nine Illinois counties.

- Prior uses, heavy systems, loading, utilities, and environmental history can drive value and closing risk.
- The purchase agreement should control deadlines, access, seller deliverables, and remedies for findings.
- Environmental review often starts with a Phase I ESA and may expand to sampling, vapor, tanks, asbestos, lead, or closure issues.
- Turn roof, slab, dock, utility, fire-protection, pavement, and drainage findings into a capital plan.
- Findings inform price, credits, escrows, repairs, insurance, indemnities, or whether to proceed.
- Owner lens: For an owner, diligence is also the start of the permanent building file. Preserve reports, permits, warranties, maintenance logs, environmental records, and repair decisions for lenders, insurers, tenants, and a future buyer.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_Renovation inspection in Vicenza, Italy. Qualified professionals can document building systems and property-specific findings._

## Why industrial diligence is different

Beyond rent, taxes and a walk-through, investigate past and current chemicals, fuels, tanks, floor drains, heavy equipment, vehicle repair, food handling, manufacturing residues and unusual utility loads.

Roof, slab, docks, sprinklers, transformers, truck courts, and drainage can affect occupancy timing and capital needs.

Use the investment diligence guide for acquisitions, and the industrial evaluation checklist and building types and specifications guide for building fit.

## Organizing the diligence period

The purchase agreement should set the diligence start, seller deliverables, access, and remedies for buyer objections. Calendar notice dates before ordering reports.

Specify access for environmental consultants, roofers, surveyors, engineers, lenders, insurers, contractors, appraisers, and utilities, including tenant coordination and sampling permissions.

Assemble the selling guide documents to ease review, not replace diligence.

- Track document status, responsible party, deadline, and open issues.
- Set insurance, safety, and escort rules for invasive or operationally sensitive inspections.
- Coordinate tenant notices and quiet hours at occupied properties.
- Allow time for follow-up testing if an initial report raises concerns.

## Environmental diligence

Scope environmental work to history, intended use, lender requirements and buyer risk tolerance. Confirm standards, reliance language and data gaps with the consultant and counsel.

### Phase I ESA and AAI

A Phase I Environmental Site Assessment is commonly prepared under ASTM E1527-21 and federal All Appropriate Inquiries concepts. The U.S. EPA All Appropriate Inquiries page explains the federal framework and links to current rules.

Scope commonly includes records, historical sources, site reconnaissance, interviews and a report of recognized environmental conditions. Users must supply specialized knowledge, commonly known information and applicable purchase-price and environmental-lien information.

AAI must be conducted or updated within one year before acquisition; certain components must be conducted or updated within 180 days. Confirm current requirements and reliance language with the consultant and counsel.

### RECs, HRECs, and CRECs

A recognized environmental condition (REC) indicates likely presence or release of hazardous substances or petroleum. A historical recognized environmental condition (HREC) generally indicates a past release addressed to the applicable standard.

A controlled recognized environmental condition (CREC) generally means a past release remains subject to controls, restrictions, or obligations. These terms can affect lender review, buyer obligations, and future use.

### Phase II sampling and vapor intrusion

A Phase II may sample soil, groundwater, soil gas, indoor air, or other media to test specific concerns. It cannot prove that no risk exists anywhere on the property.

Review vapor intrusion where volatile chemicals or petroleum releases may migrate into buildings. Qualified environmental professionals should address sampling methods, seasonal conditions, building pressure, and mitigation design.

### Asbestos, lead, PCBs, USTs, and other regulated materials

Older industrial buildings may need separate surveys for asbestos, lead paint, PCBs in equipment or caulk, underground and aboveground tanks, hydraulic lifts, sumps, and floor drains. These are often outside a basic Phase I unless added.

Ask whether targeted surveys are needed before demolition, renovation, financing, or occupancy. Removal and disposal rules affect timing and cost.

### Illinois EPA SRP and NFR letters

The voluntary Illinois EPA Site Remediation Program can yield a No Further Remediation letter for addressed conditions, not removal of every environmental risk.

Review the recorded terms, institutional controls, engineered barriers, exposure routes, and future-use limits. Counsel and the consultant should confirm whether the proposed use remains consistent with the closure.

### Landowner liability protections

Federal landowner liability protections depend on specific facts, potentially including proper AAI, continuing obligations, no affiliation issues and post-acquisition conduct.

A report is no guarantee. Review facts with environmental counsel before relying on protection.

## Physical diligence

Physical diligence covers condition, code and safety concerns, repairs, capital needs, and operational constraints. A property condition assessment may reference ASTM E2018; scope it to the asset and deal.

### Roof, structure, and slab

Review roof age, membrane, warranty, leaks, drainage, penetrations, insulation, repairs, and replacement timing. Inspect structure and slab for settlement, cracks, joints, flatness, load capacity, mezzanines, roof framing, impact, and water intrusion.

### Docks, doors, and equipment

Field-test dock levelers, bumpers, seals, shelters, overhead and drive-in doors, controls and restraints where practical. Assess safety, operations and fit for intended use.

Compare the fleet with gates, docks, truck courts, and overhead obstructions using the vehicle dimensions and turning-path reference . A qualified engineer should review swept paths and margins; cargo-box dimensions alone do not establish access.

### Mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection

Review MEP useful life, capacity, code concerns, maintenance, and tenant modifications. Confirm electrical capacity against panels, service, transformer, utility data, and equipment.

For fire protection, request sprinkler inspections, alarm records, deficiencies, hydraulic calculations, applicable fire-pump tests, and storage or commodity assumptions. Verify design with a fire-protection engineer, insurer, and authority having jurisdiction.

### Pavement, drainage, and flood

Inspect pavement, catch basins, detention, ponding, striping, curbs, and truck-wear areas for trailer, forklift, snow-removal, drainage, and yard needs.

Check local flood and drainage records and the FEMA Flood Map Service Center . FEMA maps do not replace a civil engineer's site-drainage or stormwater review.

### Accessibility, elevators, and cranes

Review accessible parking, routes, entrances, restrooms, office areas, signage, and alterations. For elevators, hoists, bridge cranes, and jib cranes, confirm records, load ratings, inspections, service contracts, and ownership.

### Deferred maintenance and capital plan

Turn inspection notes into a capital plan with timing, cost ranges, responsibility, and business impact. Separate immediate life-safety work from maintenance and future improvements.

## Title, survey, and land

Title and survey connect legal rights to physical use. The title commitment lists requirements and exceptions; the ALTA survey shows boundaries, easements, improvements, access, and encroachments.

Review access rights, shared drives, cross-parking, utilities, drainage easements, signage, covenants, and reciprocal easements. A truck entrance across another parcel needs documented rights, not just historical use.

For rail-served property, confirm agreements, switch rights, track maintenance, active service, clearance, and who controls access. Rail value depends on legal and physical service rights matching the marketing description.

## Zoning and permits

Confirm zoning district, permitted and special uses, variances, nonconforming rights, outdoor storage, parking, truck routing, screening, signage, and hours. A zoning verification letter can document the municipality's view.

Permits and certificates of occupancy document approved work and uses. Check open permits, violations, expired approvals, fire-code issues, unpermitted mezzanines, and tenant improvements needing closeout.

For local research starting points, use the nine-county hub and municipal records. For Chicago-specific research, see the Chicago commercial real estate guide .

## Operational and lease diligence for leased industrial

Verify rent-roll income, obligations, and operating rights against signed documents. Request every lease, amendment, guaranty, side letter, estoppel, SNDA, and occupancy notice.

- Estoppels: confirm rent, term, deposits, defaults, options, exclusive rights, and tenant claims.
- SNDAs: coordinate lender, buyer, and tenant rights after a foreclosure or ownership change.
- CAM reconciliations: test recoveries, caps, exclusions, reserves, management fees, and year-end balances.
- Repair obligations: identify who pays for roof, structure, HVAC, pavement, dock equipment, fire protection, and capital replacements.
- Hazardous materials clauses: compare lease rights to actual operations, permits, storage, and environmental reports.
- Parking and trailer rights: confirm allocated spaces, yard rights, storage limits, and rules for containers or fleet vehicles.

The commercial leasing guide explains why lease labels do not replace a clause-by-clause review.

## Utilities and infrastructure

Compare electricity, gas, water, sanitary and storm sewer, compressed air, fiber, and telecom with the user's equipment and occupancy schedule before commitment.

Electrical capacity may involve ComEd , the serving utility, an electrical engineer, and the equipment vendor. Confirm voltage, phase, amperage, transformer ownership, spare capacity, upgrade lead times, and shutdown requirements.

For existing or proposed battery energy storage, collect ownership and service contracts, approved plans, utility permissions, commissioning records, safety documentation and removal obligations. The BESS owner guide explains storage, peak savings, engineered backup, fire and insurance review, and standalone storage land leases. Neither a large service nor nearby transmission guarantees interconnection capacity.

For gas, water, and sewer, check meter size, pressure, discharge limits, floor drains, pretreatment, process water, fire flow, and municipal capacity. General serviceability does not confirm fiber or telecom.

## Turning findings into price, credits, escrows, or repairs

Use findings to accept risk, renegotiate, seek credits or escrow, require repairs, modify representations, obtain insurance or terminate where permitted.

Sellers should separate documented defects from buyer preferences and speculative upgrades. Buyers should distinguish routine maintenance from issues affecting value, financing, insurability, or lawful use.

Support material findings with report pages, photos, contractor proposals, municipal responses, title exceptions, lease clauses, or consultant memos.

## Diligence checklist

Adapt this checklist to property type, contract, lender, tenant, intended use and risk tolerance.

**Industrial property diligence checklist**
- Item: Purpose: Typical provider
- Phase I ESA / AAI: Review current and historical environmental risk and liability protections.: Environmental consultant and counsel.
- Phase II or targeted sampling: Test concerns from records, conditions, or Phase I findings.: Environmental consultant and laboratory.
- Asbestos, lead, PCB, tank, and regulated-material surveys: Identify handling, renovation, demolition, or closure issues.: Specialty environmental consultant.
- Property condition assessment: Evaluate systems, immediate repairs, and capital needs.: Engineer, architect, or PCA consultant.
- Roof report: Assess condition, leaks, warranty, drainage, and replacement timing.: Roof consultant or qualified contractor.
- Structural and slab review: Check load, cracks, settlement, mezzanines, cranes, and equipment impacts.: Structural engineer.
- MEP review: Confirm capacity, useful life, code concerns, and maintenance.: MEP contractors or engineers.
- Fire-protection review: Check inspections, deficiencies, design assumptions, and storage compatibility.: Fire-protection contractor, engineer, insurer, and AHJ.
- Pavement and drainage review: Assess truck areas, ponding, stormwater, catch basins, and yard surface.: Civil engineer or pavement consultant.
- Title commitment and exception documents: Identify liens, requirements, easements, covenants, and restrictions.: Title company and real estate attorney.
- Survey: Show boundaries, improvements, access, encroachments, easements, and parking/yard layout.: Licensed surveyor.
- Zoning verification: Confirm permitted use, nonconforming rights, parking, outdoor storage, and violations.: Municipality, zoning consultant, and land-use attorney.
- Lease and tenant file review: Confirm rent, term, options, obligations, recoveries, defaults, and use rights.: Real estate attorney, broker, property manager, and buyer.
- Utility confirmation: Verify service for electricity, gas, water, sewer, fire flow, and communications.: Utilities, engineers, contractors, and tenant equipment vendors.
- Capital plan and negotiation summary: Translate findings into price, credit, escrow, repair, insurance, or closing decisions.: Buyer, broker, counsel, lender, consultants, and seller.

For terminology, the Phase I ESA / AAI , ALTA survey , and title commitment glossary entries provide plain-English definitions.

> This guide is general education, not engineering, environmental, legal, tax, appraisal, brokerage, or investment advice. Verify environmental conditions, building systems, title, survey, zoning, leases, utilities, and transaction decisions with qualified professionals before acting.

Market orientation · Illinois logistics corridors

# Chicagoland industrial submarkets and logistics corridors

No rent, vacancy, pricing, or ranking claims.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Explore industrial clusters, freight infrastructure and location diligence in Illinois counties around Chicago.
- Submarket names are brokerage conventions, not legal boundaries.
- Verify each parcel’s municipality, county, zoning, truck routes, utilities, and tax district.
- Corridors often follow interstates, tollways, airports, rail, and intermodal access.
- Aurora, Elgin, Joliet, and other municipalities cross county lines; verify the parcel.
- This guide covers geography and infrastructure, not market rankings or statistics.
- Owner lens: Before a future lease or sale, test staff and shipment routes and replacement-user demand, not just distance to highways, airports, or terminals.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_The BNSF intermodal terminal in Cicero, Illinois. Verify each property’s routes and site access._

## How to use submarket labels

Submarket labels describe geography for brokers, lenders, owners and tenants, not zoning, tax districts or municipal boundaries. Providers may define “O’Hare,” “I-55” or “Joliet” differently.

Before underwriting 10,000 to 100,000 square feet, verify county and municipality through the nine-county industrial research hub . Match zoning, permitted use, truck routes, taxes and utilities to the parcel, not its marketed corridor.

### Practical use

Use labels to search and tour; use legal records for closing, financing, zoning, environmental review, and municipal approvals.

## Corridors and clusters described by geography

### O’Hare corridor

Elk Grove Village, Bensenville, Wood Dale, Franklin Park, Schiller Park, and Des Plaines connect to I-90, I-294, I-190, and O’Hare air cargo. Verify county, municipality, truck circulation, and airport-adjacent restrictions.

### North Cook and Lake County

Northbrook, Wheeling, Buffalo Grove, Lincolnshire, Libertyville, Gurnee, and Waukegan relate to I-94, US-41, and local arterials. Lake County here means Illinois, not Indiana.

### Northwest and I-90

Schaumburg, Hoffman Estates, Elgin, Huntley, and the Belvidere direction follow I-90. Boone County is outside scope; Elgin crosses county lines.

### Central DuPage, I-355 and I-88

Addison, Carol Stream, West Chicago, Glendale Heights, Lombard, Naperville, and Aurora relate to I-355, I-88, North Avenue, Roosevelt Road, and DuPage Airport. Aurora and Naperville cross county lines.

### West Cook, I-290 and inner I-55

Bedford Park, McCook, Hodgkins, Cicero, Bellwood, Melrose Park, and Northlake form an infill logistics belt near BNSF Cicero, CSX Bedford Park, and Union Pacific Global 2.

### I-55 corridor

Bolingbrook, Romeoville, Woodridge, Lemont, and Plainfield are commonly grouped along I-55, I-355, and nearby arterials across Will, DuPage, and Cook counties.

### I-80 and Joliet area

Joliet, Elwood, Channahon, Minooka, Shorewood, University Park, and Monee relate to I-80 and I-55. BNSF Logistics Park Chicago and Union Pacific Global 4 are key reference points.

### South Cook, I-57 and I-294

Alsip, Bridgeview, Chicago Heights, Harvey, Markham, Matteson, and South Holland are near I-57, I-294, I-80, and Calumet-area rail, including Norfolk Southern and CN.

### City of Chicago industrial corridors

The City of Chicago uses official industrial corridor planning and Planned Manufacturing District tools. See the Industrial Corridor Modernization Initiative .

### Kane, Kendall, DeKalb, McHenry, and Grundy outer markets

Aurora, Batavia, Geneva, St. Charles, Yorkville, Oswego, Plano, DeKalb, Sycamore, Woodstock, Crystal Lake, and Morris are smaller clusters tied to I-88, the I-39 direction, and I-80 west.

## Freight infrastructure overview

Nearby terminals or airports do not guarantee truck access, suitable zoning, loading or yard depth.

### Intermodal terminals and rail references

**Selected Chicago-area freight facilities to verify with official railroad sources**
- Facility: Railroad: Municipality or area: County: Official source
- Cicero Intermodal: BNSF: Cicero: Cook: BNSF facility listings
- Logistics Park Chicago: BNSF: Elwood: Will: BNSF facility listing
- Global 2: Union Pacific: Northlake: Cook: Union Pacific Global 2
- Global 4: Union Pacific: Joliet: Will: Union Pacific Global 4
- Bedford Park Intermodal: CSX: Bedford Park: Cook: CSX intermodal
- Landers: Norfolk Southern: Chicago: Cook: Norfolk Southern
- Chicago/Harvey terminal: CN: Harvey area: Cook: CN intermodal terminals

### Airports, interstates and tollways

**Air and highway references for industrial location review**
- Category: Examples: Source to check
- Air cargo: O’Hare cargo; Midway for airport adjacency; Chicago Rockford as a regional cargo point outside the nine-county scope.: FlyChicago cargo
- Tollways: I-90, I-294, I-355, I-88, and other Illinois Tollway facilities.: Illinois Tollway
- State and interstate routes: I-55, I-57, I-80, I-39 direction, US-41, and state-maintained arterials.: Illinois Department of Transportation

## How location factors enter underwriting

For 10,000 to 100,000 square foot industrial buildings, underwrite the actual drive, dock, labor, and approval path, not just the corridor label.

### Factors to test
- Labor access: shift timing, transit availability, parking, and commute patterns.
- Truck routes: municipal restrictions, bridge clearances, road weight limits, turning movements, and neighborhood constraints.
- Last-mile versus regional distribution: customer proximity, expressway access, driver hours, and delivery window reliability.
- Tollway costs: repeated toll exposure can affect operating cost even when the route is efficient.
- Building function: clear height, loading, truck court, yard, power, sprinklers, office ratio, and expansion area. See the industrial building guide .

Nearby infrastructure does not replace site diligence. A building near I-55 may still have a difficult left turn, shallow dock apron, or trailer-storage restrictions.

## Verification steps before relying on a submarket

Use this sequence before marketing a building, signing an LOI, or budgeting improvements.

### Checklist
- Confirm the address, PIN, county, municipality, township, school district, and fire district in the county hub .
- Verify zoning, legal nonconforming status, outdoor storage, parking, truck routes, and hours of operation with the municipality.
- Review utilities: electric service, gas, water, sanitary, stormwater, fire protection, and available capacity.
- Check access: curb cuts, easements, shared drives, rail rights, signal timing, bridge limits, and municipal truck-route maps.
- Compare the building to the user need: loading, clear height, power, office finish, yard, floor condition, and expansion land.
- Review taxes, incentives, TIFs, enterprise zones, and transfer taxes with the Illinois industrial property tax guide .

## Sources

These links are starting points for official verification. Use parcel, terminal, airport, tollway, and municipal sources together.

### Official and operator sources
- City of Chicago Industrial Corridor Modernization Initiative
- Chicago Department of Aviation cargo information
- BNSF facility listings
- Union Pacific Global 2 and Union Pacific Global 4
- CSX intermodal , Norfolk Southern , and CN intermodal terminals
- Illinois Tollway and Illinois Department of Transportation

Cross-check selling industrial property , commercial leasing , commercial investment and the glossary for transaction context.

Illinois, USA · County-by-county research

# Chicagoland industrial real estate: nine Illinois counties

Educational research, not listings or current market statistics.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Research warehouse, distribution, manufacturing, and flex property in Cook, DeKalb, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake, McHenry, and Will counties. Start with the parcel and operation, then identify the relevant authorities and records.

- Covers nine Illinois counties: Cook, DeKalb, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake, McHenry, and Will.
- Confirm county, municipality or unincorporated status, and every PIN. Authority follows the parcel.
- County sections link official planning, zoning, parcel, and assessment offices.
- Aurora, Elgin, and Joliet cross county lines. Lake County here means Illinois, not Indiana.
- Owner lens: A sale or expansion can involve separate municipal, county, fire, utility, stormwater, and tax reviews. Confirm parcel boundaries, service providers, and responsibility for each approval before committing capital.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

> Defined scope. This guide covers these nine counties in Illinois, USA. It is not an exhaustive or official definition of “Chicagoland.” Indiana and Wisconsin properties are outside this guide; Lake County here means Lake County, Illinois, not Lake County, Indiana.

_Small- and mid-bay industrial buildings in Elk Grove Village, Cook and DuPage counties, typical of the 10,000 to 100,000 SF segment._

## Establish jurisdiction before comparing locations

Record address, every property index number (PIN), county and incorporation status. Postal cities, listing labels and tax records do not establish zoning authority. Check every parcel; municipalities may cross counties and projects may span parcels.

Start with municipal planning, zoning and building staff for incorporated sites, or the county department below for unincorporated sites. Confirm shared services and separate fire, health, highway, utility and stormwater approvals. County assessment and maps can also help under municipal zoning.

GIS aids research; it is not a survey, title opinion, zoning approval or utility guarantee. Comprehensive plans state policy or future use, not current zoning or operating permission. Municipal examples orient research, not recommendations or available-space claims.

### County assessment offices

Cook has an elected assessor. In the other eight counties, township assessors typically set initial values; county supervisors of assessments or chief assessment officers supervise, equalize and publish them. County offices below provide parcels, assessment history, exemptions and appeal deadlines. Verify bills with the treasurer.

**Official assessment offices for the nine counties**
- County: Office
- Cook: Cook County Assessor
- DeKalb: DeKalb County Assessment Office (Chief County Assessment Officer)
- DuPage: DuPage County Supervisor of Assessments
- Grundy: Grundy County Supervisor of Assessments
- Kane: Kane County Supervisor of Assessments
- Kendall: Kendall County Supervisor of Assessments
- Lake: Lake County, Illinois Chief County Assessment Office
- McHenry: McHenry County Office of Assessments
- Will: Will County Supervisor of Assessments

## Cook County: distinguish Chicago from suburban authority

Chicago and suburbs such as Bedford Park require separate research. Chicago's zoning map and Department of Buildings are city resources, not countywide permitting systems. Cook County Building and Zoning directs incorporated-property inquiries to the municipality and handles unincorporated areas, with a separate role for Forest Preserve property.

For city distribution or service operations, trace the public-road approach to loading, including curb access, backing, delivery windows, pedestrian conflicts, and street-use rules. For suburban sites, verify outdoor storage and trailer parking separately from indoor warehouse permission. A Chicago mailing address or industrial tax classification settles neither question.

- Cook County Building and Zoning : county jurisdiction and building/zoning services.
- Cook County Assessor : identify parcels and assessment records; verify tax bills separately.
- Chicago zoning map and Chicago Department of Buildings : city-specific starting points.

## DeKalb County: separate mapped land use from approvals

DeKalb and Sycamore are municipal starting points; confirm sites outside municipal limits with the county. DeKalb County Community Development reviews unincorporated construction and administers county planning, zoning, subdivision, and stormwater rules.

Use the county's Property Data and Maps and Community Development maps together to identify parcels and review zoning and development layers. An enterprise-zone map or future-use designation does not establish incentive eligibility or approval for an industrial use.

For new manufacturing or warehouse expansion, define footprint, process-water needs, electrical loads, drainage changes and access. Confirm parcel service with authorities and utilities; nearby development does not reserve capacity.

- DeKalb County Assessment Office : parcel identification, assessment records, and appeal information.
- DeKalb County Community Development : planning, building, and land-use responsibilities.
- DeKalb County Property Data and Maps : parcel, tax, land-record, and Community Development map entry points.

## DuPage County: reconcile municipal limits and building fit

Research Addison and Carol Stream through their municipal departments. DuPage County Building and Zoning permits unincorporated areas; its Interactive Map Gallery links a parcel viewer.

For warehouse or office/industrial flex, compare the proposed office, storage, and production mix with approved occupancy and parking. Check whether conversion affects fire separation, accessibility, ventilation, or loading. A flexible plan does not make every activity permissible.

Plot the lot, driveway, truck court, and easements before assuming room for docks or trailer storage. Keep parcel and permit records separate across counties, even when corridor labels match.

- DuPage County Supervisor of Assessments : assessment records, exemptions, and appeal procedures.
- DuPage County Building and Zoning : building, zoning, and planning services.
- DuPage County Interactive Map Gallery : county maps and the linked Parcel Viewer.

## Grundy County: investigate site development and approval paths

Morris is a municipal starting point. For county-administered sites, Grundy County's Land Use Department separates Building, Planning and Zoning, and Environmental and Resource Conservation. Contact the office responsible for the work; a zoning inquiry is not full development review.

Planning and Zoning holds hearings for map amendments, subdivision plats, special uses and variances. Its page distinguishes committee and County Board recommendations from Zoning Board of Appeals variance decisions. Confirm relief or rezoning sequences before committing possession or construction dates.

For a distribution yard or undeveloped manufacturing site, plan for pavement, grading, drainage, outdoor storage, and emergency access. Have qualified professionals review flood maps and elevations. Vacant land or existing pavement does not establish expansion rights.

- Grundy County Supervisor of Assessments : online assessment inquiry, forms, and Board of Review information.
- Grundy County Land Use Department : department structure and building-related starting points.
- Grundy County Planning and Zoning Office : hearing types and decision paths.

## Kane County: resolve multi-county names and construction scope

Geneva is a Kane County reference point. Aurora and Elgin cross county lines; identify the parcel's county and municipal limits before ordering records or estimating taxes. Kane's map directory supports municipality, address, and parcel research.

Kane County Building and Zoning provides unincorporated-site research and permit instructions for construction, remodeling, repair, and demolition. Check whether equipment installation, mezzanines, dock changes, or production conversion need review. A prior tenant's permit does not approve your project.

Where routes cross the Fox River, test the specific crossing and approach with the intended vehicle. Check road authority, restrictions, and access rights; a mapped route does not establish legal truck access or delivery time.

- Kane County Supervisor of Assessments : parcel and assessment research for Kane County portions of a property.
- Kane County Building and Zoning Division : unincorporated property research, permit instructions, and references.
- Kane County maps : official entry point for parcel and municipality mapping.

## Kendall County: verify service authority and expansion assumptions

Yorkville and Oswego are municipal starting points. At county boundaries, verify the parcel through Kendall County GIS rather than relying on a municipal name.

Kendall's Planning, Building and Zoning Department serves unincorporated areas and the incorporated villages of Millbrook and Plattville. Confirm which office handles zoning, building, and inspection for the address.

For warehouse land or manufacturing expansion, request written utility availability, extension responsibilities, and subdivision or site-change approvals. Use the Land Resource Management Plan as context, then confirm current zoning and required relief. Budget approvals and infrastructure separately from land price.

- Kendall County Supervisor of Assessments : assessment records, township assessor contacts, and appeals.
- Kendall County Planning, Building and Zoning : service area, land-use planning, and department guidance.
- Kendall County Geographic Information Systems : official mapping and property-information entry point.

## Lake County, Illinois: use early assistance for complex projects

Waukegan and Gurnee are Lake County, Illinois examples, not Indiana's Lake County or Wisconsin. The county directs incorporated-site inquiries to cities or villages and describes permits for unincorporated sites.

Early Assistance meetings coordinate departments for complex unincorporated Lake County nonresidential projects. Bring a site and operational concept; manufacturing, warehouse use changes and flex conversion need more than square footage.

The permitting page distinguishes change-of-use, site-development, building, conditional-use, and other approvals. Ask which apply to production, earthwork, outdoor activity, or new storage. Use the county map for geographic research and confirm drainage, wetlands, and flood issues with authorities and specialists.

- Lake County, Illinois Chief County Assessment Office : assessment records, exemptions, and appeal procedures.
- Lake County Permits, Approvals and Early Assistance : unincorporated permitting and coordinated project guidance.
- Lake County, Illinois mapping and open data : official geographic-data starting point.

## McHenry County: combine land-use maps with permit history

Woodstock and Crystal Lake are municipal starting points. McHenry County Planning and Development directs incorporated-site inquiries to the city or village and handles unincorporated permitting.

McHenry GIS separates Athena property information from PlanDev zoning and land-use research. Check current zoning separately from proposed land use. Use Electronic Records Search for available closed permits and zoning petitions; request missing records and confirmation of current approvals.

For distribution or storage, review the full route, local truck access, drainage, loading-hour limits, and neighboring uses. For manufacturing conversion, compare records with equipment, wastewater, ventilation, and fire-protection needs.

- McHenry County Office of Assessments : assessment notices, parcel inquiry, and complaint deadlines.
- McHenry County Planning and Development : county permitting and land-use services.
- McHenry County GIS Interactive Maps : property and planning map directory.
- McHenry County Electronic Records Search : available permit and zoning records, not proof of current building condition.

## Will County: separate freight proximity from usable access

Romeoville is a Will County reference point. Joliet crosses into Kendall County, so verify each parcel. For incorporated sites, start with the municipality; ask county land-use staff about county-administered zoning.

Will County Current Planning and Zoning handles map amendments, special uses, variances, and building-permit zoning review, and maintains zoning maps and records. Request the district, approvals, and conditions for yards, parking, setbacks, and proposed uses; an industrial label is not project approval.

For sites marketed near freight infrastructure, verify gate-to-destination routes, terminal access, staging, queuing, and legal trailer parking. Nearby rail does not establish service or access rights. Review manufacturing utilities and process approvals separately.

- Will County Supervisor of Assessments : assessment records, exemptions, and appeal information.
- Will County Land Use Department : official department entry point.
- Will County Current Planning and Zoning : zoning applications, permit review, plans, and records.

## Match the operation in every county

- **Warehouse and storage**: Identify commodities, rack layout, storage height, slab loads, and fire-protection design. Verify usable clear height below obstructions and whether approved storage arrangements fit the inventory.
- **Distribution and logistics**: Model peak vehicle movements, dock appointments, truck turning, queuing, trailer storage, and employee access. Test routes at relevant times; neither county location nor highway proximity guarantees travel time.
- **Manufacturing**: Give reviewers equipment and process details, electrical demand, water use, discharge, emissions, noise, vibration, and operating hours. Confirm utility capacity and applicable permits before assuming an industrial building can accommodate production.
- **Flex space**: Define the office/industrial mix, customer visits, parking, occupancy classification, ventilation, and separation between uses. Existing office improvements do not establish permission for assembly, production, or storage.

Use the industrial building-fit checklist for measurements, systems, loading and inspections. County research complements it, not engineering, environmental or code specialist review.

## Build a property-specific diligence file

- Identity and authority: retain the PINs, boundary evidence, zoning designation, responsible offices, and written responses about the exact use.
- Records and site risk: collect approvals, permit history, title and survey information, access rights, drainage documents, and tax records for every parcel. Use the correct county assessor and treasurer, not Cook County by default.
- Flood and environmental review: start with the FEMA Flood Map Service Center and EPA All Appropriate Inquiries guidance , then commission appropriate site-specific work. Maps and an assessment are not guarantees that all risk is absent.
- Cost and schedule: itemize improvements, utility upgrades, permit dependencies, and responsibility for ongoing maintenance. Use the leasing guide or purchase-diligence guide for transaction-specific questions.

Record the source, access date, parcel searched, verified finding, and unresolved question. Official pages and applications can change; if a map or portal is unavailable, contact the named county department. For the broader research process, see commercial property research .

> This hub is general education, not a listing service, market ranking, appraisal, or legal, tax, engineering, environmental, or investment advice. It makes no claim about available inventory, rents, returns, incentives, or professional credentials. Obtain property-specific advice and current source documents before making a commitment.

Owner guide · Illinois industrial tax diligence

# Property taxes on Illinois industrial real estate

Educational, not tax or legal advice.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

How tax bills, reassessments, incentives and lease pass-throughs affect Illinois’s small and midsize industrial assets.
- Tax flows from assessment through equalization, levy, rate, billing, and collection.
- Cook uses classifications; collar counties generally follow the state assessment standard.
- For a sale, model the likely future bill, not just the seller’s current bill.
- Review incentive, zone, and TIF documents.
- Leases should allocate appeals, refunds, escrows, and reassessment risk.
- Owner lens: An appeal does not stop bills, lender escrows, or lease pass-throughs. Budget payments separately and calendar filings, payments, and tenant reconciliations.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_Industrial parcels in Elk Grove Village, Illinois. Verify parcel boundaries, PINs, assessments and tax districts in official records._

_National Park Service staff review plans at Cape Cod National Seashore. Organize your property’s tax evidence and deadlines using official county records._

## How Illinois property tax works at a high level

Illinois industrial property taxes are local, within a state-supervised system: assessment, equalization, levy, rate, bill, and collection. Check each step against the parcel’s county, municipality, school district, and special districts.

### From assessment to bill
- **Assessment**: The assessor estimates taxable value. Outside Cook County, Illinois generally assesses at 33⅓% of fair cash value before equalization and exemptions; Cook County uses its own classification levels.
- **Equalization**: An equalization factor, or multiplier, may adjust assessments for greater uniformity. See assessed value and equalization factor .
- **Levy**: Taxing districts set levies for schools, municipalities, counties, parks, libraries, fire, sanitary, and other local services.
- **Rate and extension**: The county clerk extends rates against equalized assessed value; the assessor does not set the rate.
- **Bill and collection**: The county treasurer bills and collects. Illinois taxes are commonly paid in installments after the tax year; confirm dates with the county treasurer.

## Cook County versus the collar counties

### Cook County classification

Cook County's elected assessor assigns each PIN a classification that determines its assessment level. The assessor says office, industrial, and retail buildings typically have a 25% level of assessment . Residential and multifamily differ, so use care with mixed-use and conversion assumptions.

Cook’s regional triennial reassessment cycle requires checking the current township calendar before relying on old values.

### Collar-county assessment

In DeKalb, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake, McHenry, and Will, a township assessor commonly makes the initial assessment, reviewed by the county supervisor of assessments. The state guide explains the 33⅓% standard and equalization; county pages give local deadlines and forms.

## Reading an industrial tax bill

### Fields to review

**Common fields on an industrial tax bill**
- Field: Why it matters
- PIN or parcel number: Industrial sites may have multiple PINs for building, yard, parking, or excess land. Confirm all parcels transfer.
- Assessed value and EAV: Shows the assessment base before rates. Compare it with notices, appeals, and the assessor property card.
- Equalization factor: The multiplier can change the taxable base even when the local assessment appears unchanged.
- Exemptions: Industrial property usually has few owner exemptions; verify any exemption, incentive, or special assessment before assuming it continues.
- Taxing districts: School, municipal, county, park, fire, library, and special districts drive the combined rate.
- Tax rate and extensions: The rate converts EAV into the bill. High rates can change buyer proceeds and tenant pass-throughs.
- TIF notation: A TIF district can affect how incremental taxes are allocated and how incentives are documented.

## Reassessment, appeals and deadlines

Appeals have strict deadlines; missing an assessor, Board of Review, or state filing date can defer the issue to a later tax year. Build a tax calendar during diligence.

### Appeal forums
- Assessor review: informal or formal review at the assessor level, depending on the county and township calendar.
- County Board of Review: county-level appeal after assessment publication. In Cook, the Cook County Board of Review has its own filing rules.
- State or court review: after the county level, an owner may evaluate the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board or circuit court with counsel.

### Evidence for industrial property

Evidence may include income, comparable sales and recent arms-length transactions, vacancy or functional issues, rent-roll limits, deferred maintenance, environmental conditions, and constraints such as loading, clear height, sprinklers, power, or yard usability.

## Cook County incentive classifications for industrial property

Cook’s most discussed industrial incentive, Class 6b , encourages new facilities, rehabilitation and abandoned-building reuse, according to the assessor.

### Class 6b basics

The current Cook County Class 6b bulletin sets the reduced assessment at 10% for the first ten years, 15% in year eleven, and 20% in year twelve , subject to ordinance and application requirements. Review the application, municipal resolution, occupancy history, abandonment facts, renewal, and compliance, not just the shorthand.

### Incentive diligence questions

Confirm approval, transferability, renewal, municipal resolution, compliance conditions, and lease allocation of benefit, refunds, and appeal control.

## Enterprise zones and TIF districts

An enterprise zone may offer project-specific incentives, not automatic eligibility. Illinois DCEO directs applicants for building-material sales tax exemption certificates to each zone’s local administrator.

A TIF district is different. A tax increment financing district can redirect eligible growth in tax revenue for public purposes within a district. It may appear on local maps, redevelopment agreements, or tax bills. In both cases, read the governing documents, expiration dates, and assignment rules.

## Taxes in underwriting and leases

### Lease controls
- NNN leases : confirm whether real estate taxes pass through, whether reassessment is included, and whether refunds are shared.
- Appeals: decide who may file, who pays professionals, and how settlements affect tenants.
- Escrows: lenders may require tax escrows; buyers should align closing prorations and lender reserves.
- Transfer taxes: Illinois, county, and municipal transfer taxes may apply. Chicago has its own finance department and rules. See transfer tax .

For sale-process context, see Illinois and Cook County considerations and pricing approach .

## A seller’s and buyer’s tax checklist

**Industrial property tax diligence checklist**
- Topic: Review
- Parcels: List every PIN and confirm against deed, survey, zoning lot, and operating site.
- Current taxes: Review bills, payment status, prorations, escrows, and delinquencies.
- Assessments: Compare notices, classifications, equalization factors, and reassessment scenarios.
- Appeals: Disclose open matters; verify deadlines, evidence, and lease refund clauses.
- Incentives: Confirm applications, ordinances, approvals, renewals, transferability, and clawbacks.
- Leases: Check pass-through, refund, contest, and reassessment language.

## How can an Illinois owner manage property taxes year-round?

Keep every PIN, property card, area, use, classification, assessment notice, current and prior bill, lease, vacancy record and capital-condition evidence. Correct factual errors with the responsible office. Appeals address assessments; assessors neither set district levies nor guarantee bills.

### Cook cycle versus filing windows

Cook reassesses regions every three years, with appeals and changed-property reviews between mailings. Use the current township calendar for notice and appeal dates, not town names. Track the Board of Review window separately. Collar counties use county assessment publications, local Board rules and annual equalization, not Cook’s cycle.

### Assessor, Board of Review and PTAB are different steps

Start with local assessor review where available, then check county Board of Review filing rules. A PTAB appeal normally follows a Board decision; its filing instructions describe a 30-day period and decision/notification rules, including Cook-specific transmittal information. Have counsel confirm the trigger, entity representation, forms, evidence, and alternatives. PTAB recommends an appraisal for commercial and industrial appeals; asking prices alone are not equivalent evidence.

Calendar notice, filing, evidence, professional-engagement, decision, and further-review dates. An appeal does not necessarily suspend payments; confirm payment and refund handling with counsel and the treasurer.

### Budget the bill and tenant allocation, not only an appeal result

Document a base case and higher-tax scenario for reassessment, equalization, levies, and incentive expiration. Do not count an unawarded reduction as savings. Track accrued taxes, installments, lender escrows, and closing prorations separately to avoid double-counting.

Check each lease's recoverable taxes, caps, appeal fees, refund sharing, and post-sale responsibility. A gross-lease owner may bear increases that a net-lease owner partly recovers; incentives may benefit tenants. Update the NOI bridge and cash budget .

## Class 6b, Class 7 and Class 8: which program fits?

The Cook County Assessor's incentive directory supplies the governing eligibility bulletins and application forms. A reduced assessment classification is not a grant or an automatic percentage reduction of the tax bill. Confirm municipal support, project eligibility, deadlines, continued use, ownership changes and compliance before underwriting it.

**Program purpose, not a determination of eligibility**
- Class: General purpose: Owner diligence
- 6b: Industrial development, rehabilitation and reutilization of qualifying abandoned industrial buildings: Industrial use, work/occupancy history, municipal resolution and remaining schedule
- 7a / 7b: Qualifying commercial projects in areas needing commercial development; project-cost and feasibility requirements distinguish the classes: Not a substitute industrial class; check the current bulletin's category and development-cost rules
- 8: Industrial/commercial development in qualifying areas experiencing severe economic stagnation: Area designation, project conditions and local support; not every Cook property qualifies

Model income and taxes with and without incentives, especially at expiration or renewal. Document approval, continuation and tenant recovery with municipal staff, the Assessor and qualified tax counsel; do not promise savings.

## Illinois owner tax questions

### How can I lower commercial property taxes in Illinois?

Check parcel characteristics and assessment evidence, then file with the correct assessor or Board of Review within its calendar. Review further PTAB or court options with counsel. An assessment change does not guarantee a proportional tax-bill change because rates, levies and equalization also matter.

### Does a Cook County incentive transfer automatically on sale?

Do not assume it. Verify approval documents, the remaining schedule, ownership/use requirements and current renewal or compliance rules with the Assessor and municipality before pricing the benefit.

## Official sources

### State and regional sources
- Illinois Department of Revenue and Publication 136
- Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board
- Illinois DCEO Enterprise Zone Program
- City of Chicago Department of Finance

### Nine-county assessment offices

Assessment office links: Cook , DeKalb , DuPage , Grundy , Kane , Kendall , Lake , McHenry , and Will . Cook-specific billing and review sources: Treasurer and Board of Review .

> This guide is general education, not legal, tax, appraisal, accounting, brokerage, or investment advice. Property tax rules, assessment notices, appeal deadlines, incentives, and transfer taxes change. Verify the parcel, current year, office calendar, lease language, and transaction documents with qualified professionals before acting.

Owner guide · Chicagoland industrial sale preparation

# Selling an industrial property in Chicagoland

Educational, not a valuation or listing.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Prepare a 10,000 to 100,000 square foot industrial property for sale in the nine-county Illinois market.

- Buyers include owner-users, private investors, 1031 exchange buyers, and smaller institutions or funds.
- Leased buildings are underwritten on income, term, credit, and expenses; vacant ones on utility and financing fit.
- Value reflects function and risk: loading, clear height, systems, zoning, environmental history, leases, and deferred maintenance.
- Organized records and a confidentiality plan can reduce diligence friction.
- Owner lens: Compare net proceeds, not just price: include debt payoff and prepayment costs, transaction expenses, tax planning, repair credits, and any leaseback rent and obligations.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_Industrial buildings in Elk Grove Village, Illinois. Regional illustration, not a listing or a transaction attributed to Pavlo Rospopa._

## Who buys this size range

Occupancy, function, location, financing and timing shape buyers for 10,000 to 100,000 square feet.

- Owner-users: companies occupying the property for warehouse, distribution, manufacturing, service, or flex operations.
- Private investors: local or regional buyers seeking income, vacancy upside, or long-term control.
- 1031 exchange buyers: investors using a tax-deferred exchange under IRC Section 1031.
- Small institutional or fund buyers: professional buyers focused on credit, scale, lease term, and repeatable features.

Leased assets may appeal to investors; vacant ones may attract owner-users who value control over current income.

## How buyers underwrite

### Leased buildings

For leased property, buyers review the rent roll, leases, NOI, income durability, term, WALT, tenant credit, options, recoveries, and landlord duties.

They also check whether taxes, insurance, CAM, repairs, management fees, and capital items pass through or remain with the owner.

### Vacant or owner-user buildings

Vacant-building buyers assess function, replacement cost, timing, financing and improvements. Clear height, loading, power, office ratio, truck movement and code compliance may outweigh the rent roll.

Owner-users may consider conventional financing or SBA 504 loans . Verify eligibility and terms with the SBA, a lender, and qualified advisors.

For building-fit questions, see the industrial building evaluation guide .

## What drives value in this segment

Buyers value buildings that meet a clear operating need, not square footage alone.

**Common value drivers for 10,000 to 100,000 square foot industrial assets**
- Category: What buyers review
- Building function: Clear height, loading, truck court, columns, office percentage, floor plan, and expansion potential.
- Systems and condition: Roof, HVAC, slab, fire protection, lighting, docks, power, and deferred maintenance.
- Site and access: Outdoor storage, trailer parking, circulation, ingress, egress, utilities, and drainage.
- Legal and records: Zoning, permits, occupancy certificates, title, survey, easements, and environmental history.
- Income profile: Lease structure, rent, recovery language, obligations, remaining term, options, and credit.

The nine-county research hub helps identify parcel, zoning, and assessment offices.

## Preparing the document file

Organize documents before marketing to avoid delays in offers, financing, title, environmental review and closing.

**Industrial property seller document checklist**
- Document: Why it matters
- Leases and amendments: Confirm rent, term, options, use, maintenance, and assignment terms.
- Rent roll: Summarizes tenants, spaces, rents, deposits, options, and dates.
- Estoppels and SNDAs: Support tenant and lender confirmation.
- Operating statements: Show two to three years of income, expenses, and recoveries.
- Tax bills and assessment notices: Support tax, appeal, and reassessment review.
- CAM reconciliations: Show common-cost billing and settlement.
- Phase I ESA and environmental reports: Identify environmental diligence and unresolved issues.
- ALTA survey and title commitment: Support review of boundaries, easements, and exceptions.
- Roof, HVAC, and fire-protection reports: Document condition, inspections, repairs, and recommended work.
- Warranties and service records: Support capital work, coverage, and maintenance claims.
- Permits and certificates of occupancy: Confirm approved work, occupancy, and use history.
- Zoning verification: Documents permitted uses, parking, storage, and constraints.
- Floor plans and site plan: Show layout, docks, office area, yard, parking, and access.
- Service contracts: Show snow, landscaping, security, waste, maintenance, and utilities.
- Environmental and regulatory records: Cover permits, tanks, spills, notices, and closure documents.

## Physical preparation before marketing

Prepare the site for inspection.

- Address obvious deferred maintenance where practical, or price and disclose it.
- Clean warehouse areas, mechanical rooms, offices, loading areas, and yard.
- Replace missing lighting, repair trip hazards, and label key electrical or utility areas.
- Organize roof, HVAC, dock, fire-protection, and paving records for recent capital work.
- Confirm what personal property, racks, equipment, and fixtures are included or excluded.

For leased buildings, coordinate access with the tenant to protect operations and inform buyers.

## Pricing approach

A broker opinion supports marketing and pricing, not a formal appraisal for a defined purpose, standard, date and client.

For leased industrial property, buyers often discuss cap rates: NOI divided by the rate indicates value before deal-specific adjustments.

> Illustration only, not market data. If placeholder NOI is $300,000 and the placeholder cap rate is 6.0%, the arithmetic is $300,000 ÷ 6.0% = $5,000,000. Actual value depends on property-specific income, risk, lease terms, building condition, financing, and current buyer demand.

For vacant or owner-user property, pricing may be tested against sales, replacement cost, renovation cost, timing, and alternatives.

## Typical sale process

Processes, timing, and outcomes vary.

- Prep: gather records, resolve questions, set pricing, and define confidentiality rules.
- Marketing or confidential offering: target buyers and control information release.
- Tours: coordinate access, tenant notice, operations, and safety.
- Offers and LOI: compare price, deposits, contingencies, diligence, closing conditions, and buyer credibility.
- PSA negotiation: document representations, obligations, remedies, and timelines in the purchase agreement.
- Due diligence and inspection: buyers review leases, title, survey, zoning, environmental, physical, and financial records.
- Financing contingency: if applicable, lenders review collateral, borrower, leases, appraisal, environmental reports, and title.
- Closing: finalize conditions, funds, deeds, prorations, notices, possession, and post-closing duties.

The commercial investment diligence guide explains buyer-side items sellers should anticipate.

## Illinois and Cook County considerations

Cook County reassesses real property on a triennial cycle. Confirm current assessment status, appeal periods, and property-specific records with the Cook County Assessor .

Transfer taxes may apply at state, county, and municipal levels. Verify current requirements with official sources such as the Illinois Department of Revenue and, for Chicago property, the City of Chicago Department of Finance .

Do not rely on rates from old closing statements or summaries. Verify property-specific municipal rules and exemptions before signing.

## Sale-leaseback and 1031 exchange planning

### Sale-leaseback

A sale and leaseback frees owner-user capital without moving the business; the seller becomes a tenant with lease obligations.

Buyers underwrite rent, term, renewal options, maintenance, credit, and ability to pay. Negotiate the lease as carefully as the sale.

### 1031 exchange planning

Plan a 1031 exchange before closing. IRC Section 1031 generally sets a 45-day identification period and 180-day exchange period, subject to statutory rules.

Use a qualified intermediary and tax advisor. Start with the IRS and confirm the structure, deadlines, related-party rules, replacement property, and documentation before relying on exchange treatment.

## Confidentiality with tenants and employees

Buyers need occupied-building information, but premature rumors can affect tenants and employees, including an owner-user’s continuing business.

- Decide what information is public, what requires a signed confidentiality agreement, and what waits until a serious buyer is qualified.
- Limit tenant contact unless lease review, estoppels, tours, or lender diligence require it.
- Schedule tours around operations, safety rules, and sensitive business areas.
- Prepare a communication plan for employees if the business occupies the property.

Confidentiality protects process, operations and accuracy, not concealment of material issues.

## Thinking about selling?

Pavlo Rospopa specializes in 10,000 to 100,000 square foot industrial investment sales across Cook, DeKalb, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake, McHenry and Will counties. Contact Pavlo Rospopa for a second opinion on your building or timing.

Connect on LinkedIn Marcus & Millichap advisor page

> This guide is general education, not legal, tax, engineering, environmental, appraisal, brokerage, or investment advice. Verify property records, taxes, zoning, environmental matters, loan programs, and transaction documents with qualified professionals before acting.

## Planning an industrial property exit for retirement

Compare holding with professional management, selling for liquid proceeds and a qualifying 1031 exchange before choosing a retirement date. Estimate cash after loan payoff, sale costs and taxes, and test lease rollover, major capital work and refinancing risk. If your company occupies the building, coordinate the business sale and future lease separately.

The retirement exit guide explains why a 1031 exchange is not an IRA rollover, how retaining a building changes your workload and concentration, and which questions to bring to tax, financial and estate advisers.

Before closing, review depreciation recapture and the sale gain example and lazy 1031 and DST exchange choices . Mortgage payoff changes sale cash, not ordinarily taxable gain, and less management can bring fees, restricted liquidity and sponsor risk.

Acquisition preparation

# Commercial investment and purchase diligence

Educational framework, not an investment recommendation.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Evaluate Chicago-area commercial or industrial property by function, documented income, financing and capital needs. Price alone shows neither risks nor total cash required.

- State the purpose first: owner-use, rental income, or redevelopment each needs different underwriting.
- Underwrite signed leases, collections, expenses, and capital needs, not the marketing summary.
- Test financing terms and downside cases explicitly; a lender’s approval is not your diligence.
- Organize legal, zoning, physical, environmental, tax, and tenancy reviews before contract deadlines expire.
- Owner lens: Review entity authority, partner consent rights, guaranties, capital-call obligations, and loan covenants alongside property economics; a strong asset does not remove ownership-level liquidity risk.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_BNSF intermodal terminal in Cicero, Cook County. Freight infrastructure shapes demand, but a building’s own access still has to be verified._

## Define the acquisition’s purpose

Owner-users need business fit; investors need documented tenancy and cash flow. Redevelopment adds approval, construction, timing and leasing risks. Define purpose, hold period, capital budget and acceptable downside before comparing.

Compare owner-user costs with a realistic lease alternative, including financing, taxes, insurance, repairs, improvements and committed liquidity. For industrial assets, confirm operational suitability .

## Underwrite the documents, not the headline

- Rent roll and leases: reconcile tenants, occupied areas, rent, deposits, expirations, options, concessions and amendments to signed documents.
- Collections: separate scheduled from collected rent; identify arrears and disputes.
- Expenses: verify taxes, insurance, maintenance, management, utilities and recoveries from records, not just the marketing summary.
- Capital: estimate repairs, replacements, tenant improvements and leasing costs separately; each affects cash needs.
- Vacancy and rollover: allow for downtime, concessions and replacement-tenant costs.
- **Net operating income (NOI)**: Generally property income less operating expenses, before debt service and income taxes. Capital expenditures and some reserve treatments are usually separate; document the convention in each comparison.
- **Capitalization rate**: NOI divided by price or value on the stated basis. Projected and current documented NOI produce different rates; neither guarantees a return.
- **Cash flow to equity**: Accounts for financing and capital cash needs beyond NOI. Purchase costs, principal repayment, sale costs and taxes also affect the outcome.

Label projected rent and resale value as assumptions supported by evidence. An asking price or optimistic pro forma is not a completed comparable transaction.

## Test financing and downside explicitly

Review rate, amortization, maturity, recourse, covenants, reserves, fees, prepayment terms and any balloon payment. Lender approval does not replace your diligence.

DSCR compares defined income with required debt service. Confirm each lender’s definitions and requirements; no universal threshold applies here.

- What if a major tenant leaves or stops paying?
- Can the budget absorb higher taxes, insurance or an unexpected roof replacement?
- What if refinancing costs more or yields less at maturity?
- How much equity is needed if approvals, construction or leasing run late?
- What if sale proceeds are lower or the property takes longer to sell?

Compare a documented base case with explicit downside cases. Appreciation, refinancing and exit liquidity are not certain.

## Debt yield, DSCR and refinancing costs

Debt yield divides defined annual NOI by loan balance. Unlike DSCR, rates and amortization do not directly change it, but lender income adjustments matter. LTV uses value; DSCR uses debt service. Multiple tests may limit proceeds; no universal qualifying threshold exists.

Illustrative only: $300,000 NOI / $3,000,000 debt = 10% debt yield. With $240,000 annual debt service, DSCR is 1.25; at an assumed $5,000,000 value, LTV is 60%. These are arithmetic examples, not a Chicago loan quote or approval.

Before refinancing, obtain payoff, prepayment charges, proposed rate, amortization, lender and appraisal fees, escrows and reserves. Calculate proceeds after payoff and costs. Lower appraisals or shorter leases may require new equity despite current debt coverage. Test the gap in the owner budget .

For valuation and cash flow, see the OCC Commercial Real Estate Lending handbook , NOI guide and DCF guide . Property income, equity cash flow and taxable income are different measures.

_Industrial buildings in Elk Grove Village, Illinois. Review tenant exposure, lease rollover, capital requirements and financing together._

## Organize diligence before deadlines expire

- Legal and title: have counsel and title professionals review ownership, exceptions, survey matters, easements, access, contracts, deadlines and remedies.
- Use and approvals: confirm zoning, permitted activity, occupancy and building requirements, and approval conditions. See the Chicago property-research checklist .
- Physical condition: commission asset-appropriate inspections of the roof, structure, systems, pavement and other material components; turn findings into a timed capital plan.
- Environmental: consult an environmental professional on appropriate assessment, historical uses and further investigation. A Phase I is no guarantee that contamination is absent.
- Tax and insurance: verify parcel history and obtain advice and quotes for the proposed ownership and use; do not assume seller costs continue.
- Tenancy and closing: review leases, amendments, appropriate tenant confirmations, deposits, rent prorations, service contracts and closing documents.

EPA’s All Appropriate Inquiries guidance describes a framework relevant to certain environmental-liability protections. An assessment alone does not establish eligibility; timing, purchaser status and continuing obligations require professional advice.

For industrial acquisitions, the Chicagoland nine-county Illinois hub covers local research beyond Chicago and Cook County. Match each PIN to its county and authority; distinguish current zoning from planned land use before underwriting expansion or a tenant’s operation.

## How does CRE investing fit a retirement plan?

Distinguish a taxable investment for future retirement income from property held in an IRA or employer plan. Account ownership changes title, payment paths, borrowing, related-party restrictions and distributions. Property cash must cover debt, capital and leasing costs before funding household spending.

The CRE retirement planning guide compares IRA, Roth, Solo 401(k) and other plans; prohibited transactions and UBIT; and RMD liquidity, diversification, Illinois taxes and succession. Ask qualified tax and plan advisers about eligibility before an offer, loan guarantee or related-business lease.

The federal and Illinois tax guide distinguishes passive from portfolio income and covers cost segregation, straight-line depreciation, lazy 1031, recapture and inherited basis. Underwrite the investment before treating tax deferral as a reason to buy.

## Official sources for verification

- Cook County Assessor and Cook County Treasurer : assessment and tax research for Cook County parcels.
- EPA: All Appropriate Inquiries : environmental due-diligence background and limitations.
- FEMA Flood Map Service Center : mapped flood-hazard information.
- Chicago Department of Buildings : city building and permitting resources.

Review commercial lease terms and obligations when assessing a leased investment or comparing ownership with renting.

> This guide is not an appraisal, securities solicitation, forecast, or legal, tax, or investment advice. Consult qualified advisers and verify the transaction’s facts. No return, financing outcome, or property availability is promised.
