Industrial owner technology and diligence

# Battery energy storage systems: an industrial owner's guide

Reviewed October 8, 2026 . General property education, not engineering design, emergency instructions, an investment recommendation or a guarantee of approvals or savings.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

A BESS stores electricity for later use. For warehouses, manufacturers and landowners, value depends on the meter, load profile, utility rules, safety design and contract, not just battery size. Learn about operation, purchases and storage leases.

- BESS means battery energy storage system, sometimes written B.E.S.S. It stores energy; it does not create free electricity.
- kW describes power; kWh describes stored energy. Both matter, along with usable capacity and losses.
- Reducing a short billing peak is different from moving energy between hours or backing up a building.
- A grid connected battery does not automatically work during an outage. Safe islanded operation and critical loads require specific engineered capability.
- Utility approval, zoning and fire approval are separate. Export permissions and tariff economics must be confirmed.
- Owner lens: Identify who pays capital costs, receives meter savings and owes removal and restoration. Tenant savings do not automatically become landlord NOI.

## Evaluate the property before the equipment proposal

Discuss your industrial property's ownership, tenant and sale considerations with Pavlo Rospopa. Use qualified electrical engineers, the serving utility, fire officials, insurers and counsel for a BESS project.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_Stationary battery storage containers in Rheineck, Switzerland. This photograph is an equipment example, not a recommended product or site design._

## How does a battery energy storage system work?

A BESS stores electricity and releases it on command. Grid or onsite generation charges batteries; conversion and auxiliary equipment consume energy. Many commercial systems use lithium ion, but chemistry, equipment, performance and hazards vary.

**The battery cabinet is only one part of the system**

- Part: What it does: Owner question
- Cells, modules and racks: Store energy electrochemically: What chemistry, usable capacity, warranties and degradation limits apply?
- Battery management system (BMS): Monitors conditions such as cell voltage and temperature and coordinates protective limits: How are faults reported, logged and handled by qualified operators?
- Power conversion system/inverter: Converts battery DC and site/grid AC as the system design permits: What power rating and approved grid operating modes apply?
- Energy management system (EMS): Schedules charge/discharge using meter, tariff, reserve and operating constraints: Who controls dispatch, data access and remote changes?
- Thermal management and protection: Manage operating temperature and provide required detection/protection functions: What inspection, maintenance and safety documentation are required?
- Site electrical and communications equipment: Connect the system to the meter, loads and utility through engineered protection: What upgrades, outages, cybersecurity and utility approvals are included?

The converter supplies permitted loads or authorized exports. The EMS sets charging, discharge timing and output within battery, tariff and project limits; the BMS monitors battery conditions. Neither replaces a building fire alarm or utility export permission.

Solar and storage can connect on the AC or DC side. An engineer must verify compatibility, controls, protection and metering; not every battery suits existing solar. This guide provides no wiring, installation or emergency procedures.

## What is the difference between kW, kWh and storage duration?

kW measures delivery rate; kWh measures energy. Power alone does not establish duration. At larger scales, 1 MW equals 1,000 kW and 1 MWh equals 1,000 kWh.

Illustration: 1,000 kWh of delivered energy at a constant 250 kW lasts four hours ideally. With only 800 kWh available after reserves and capacity limits, duration is 3.2 hours before any losses outside that measurement boundary. Actual runtime varies; usable battery DC energy is not the same as delivered AC energy.

Specify nominal and usable capacity, beginning and end of life, and measurement at cells, inverter or meter. Account for temperature, HVAC and control loads, efficiency, cycling, standby time, reserves and degradation. Temperature, equipment ratings and state of charge can also limit power.

Round trip efficiency compares returned and charging energy at defined boundaries; batteries return less than they take in. Aging and cycling generally reduce capacity. Warranties can limit years, throughput, cycles, temperature and operating conditions. Replacement or augmentation may require approvals, downtime and disposal planning.

## What can BESS do for an industrial building?

### Reduce a billing peak, if the tariff rewards it

Peak shaving discharges during chargeable demand peaks, such as manufacturing starts, refrigeration, compressors or synchronized charging. Billing intervals, demand ratchets, peak windows and charges determine the saving. Recharging can create a new peak.

### Shift energy between hours

Cheap charging and later discharge can save when rate spreads exceed losses, degradation and other costs. Flat tariffs offer no automatic time arbitrage. Wholesale and tenant retail rates may differ, as may export credits, incentives and import prices.

### Use more onsite solar or manage export

Metering and controls govern solar shifting to later loads. Compare self consumption and permitted export compensation; storing every excess kWh may not pay. Design and utility rules may permit independent battery and solar operation.

### Support selected loads during an outage, only when designed for it

Grid tied operation does not automatically provide backup. Engineer utility isolation, suitable inverters and controls, protection, switching and approved islanding. Specify critical loads, starting surges, outage duration, reserves and restart behavior; battery size alone cannot assure instantaneous or motor starting power.

Backup reserves reduce bill savings capacity. Study generator, solar and battery integration separately. Emergency and legally required standby loads must meet applicable rules; a vendor's backup label does not replace required systems. Follow approved procedures, never improvised reconnection.

### Provide grid services under a separate agreement

Approved storage may serve demand response or utility and market programs. Verify enrollment, dispatch, telemetry, penalties, revenue, compatible uses and performance risk allocation; projections can double count power, energy or hours.

## Is an onsite battery the same as leasing land for grid storage?

**Two property opportunities with different economics**

- Model: Primary purpose: Property owner diligence
- Behind the meter onsite BESS: Serve the facility account, manage bills or support engineered resilience: Interval data, tenant meter rights, tariff, equipment space, financing and savings allocation
- Front of the meter grid project: Store and deliver energy for grid/market services under applicable permissions: Developer credit, transmission/distribution access, permitting, options, land rent, easements and decommissioning

Contracts govern grid income; landlords typically receive land rent, not automatic market profit or cheaper building power. Approved onsite storage may also export. Neither label decides interconnection or revenue rules.

A nearby substation, large service or vacant yard proves neither capacity nor approval. Feasibility, upgrades, queues, zoning, access, community and safety constraints can block projects. Set milestones, payments and termination rights to prevent a long, inexpensive option tying up leasing, truck circulation or sale.

## How should an owner evaluate battery savings and costs?

Collect representative annual bills and interval data, more for seasonal or operational changes. Verify supply and delivery tariffs, meter ownership, billing intervals, ratchets, import, export and demand response contracts. Compare efficiency, controls and load scheduling before buying storage.

Hypothetical example, not a ComEd quote: at $15 per kW per month, reliably reducing chargeable demand by 100 kW in each of 12 months saves $18,000 annually. Reducing one isolated peak does not establish that monthly result.

Subtract $4,000 charging/auxiliary energy, $3,000 service/software and $2,000 replacement reserve funding: annual cash benefit before financing and tax is $9,000. A $180,000 net installed cost, with no incentive, gives 20 years simple payback. These invented assumptions are not a proposal, service life or recommendation.

Model degradation, replacement timing, discounting, tariffs, availability, contract term, financing, taxes and residual/removal costs. Reserve funding is cash planning, not automatically a deduction; avoid double counting funded replacement. Value resilience separately through a documented interruption scenario, not a bill credit.

Itemize civil works, electrical upgrades, engineering, permits, equipment, commissioning, software, communications, safety, maintenance, insurance and end of life costs. Identify warranty exclusions, spare parts and response duties. Incentives and federal clean electricity and storage credits depend on project and taxpayer: confirm eligibility, ownership, timing, labor, sourcing, elections and recapture with tax counsel, not a quoted percentage. The IRS Section 48E overview does not establish eligibility.

Utility paying tenants may receive the savings. Gross leases can reduce landlord bills; net leases can also reduce reimbursements. Neither gross savings nor equipment cost automatically equals the NOI effect. See NOI , DCF and energy cost controls .

## What utility and permit questions apply in Illinois?

Identify the serving utility and local jurisdiction; ComEd does not serve all Illinois properties. PJM/MISO processes depend on connection location and type. Retail utility approval and regional market participation are separate.

- Utility screen: confirm voltage, service, transformer, proposed power, charging source, export/nonexport mode, metering and required application/studies. Do not assume nonexport removes all interconnection requirements.
- Site and title screen: review zoning, permitted use, setbacks, easements, flood/drainage, access, loading, fire apparatus routes and landlord/lender rights.
- Code and fire screen: confirm applicable editions, amendments, permits, studies and submittals with the authority having jurisdiction.
- Financial screen: identify study deposits, upgrade costs, procurement conditions, deadlines, tariff permissions and who owns equipment or improvements.
- Operating screen: establish dispatch, inspections, communications, emergency planning, utility authorization and ongoing compliance before operation.

Use the serving utility's official channels and Illinois Commerce Commission information with an experienced engineer. For ComEd accounts, review its DER interconnection guidelines and current rates and tariffs ; confirm updates, the applicable interconnection category, export eligibility, participation and deadlines directly. A submitted application or queue position is not operating approval.

For standalone/wholesale projects, confirm applicable PJM or MISO and utility processes. Nearby transmission does not guarantee connection. Zoning does not supply capacity; utility approval does not waive building/fire requirements.

## What safety and siting issues should an industrial owner understand?

Battery systems present fire, electrical, thermal and chemical hazards. Lithium ion thermal runaway can spread between cells, release heat and flammable or toxic gases, and reignite. Address credible hazards in design and emergency plans; listings and outdoor siting do not eliminate risk.

UL 9540 certifies system equipment safety; UL 9540A tests thermal runaway fire propagation. Reports are not universal safety passes or permits. Professionals must review complete systems, installations and matching evidence. Edition 6 installation level testing adds pass/fail criteria January 1, 2027; criteria vary by edition and level. See UL's explanation .

NFPA 855 and fire/building/electrical requirements depend on locally adopted editions, amendments, equipment and installation. Confirm documentation, location, separation, access, detection/protection, emergency plans and hazard analysis with officials. No universal setback, quantity exemption or suppression method is supplied here.

Preserve circulation, exits and fire access. Review trucks, flooding, drainage, cooling noise, neighbors, ventilation/gas hazards, foundations, security and signs. Indoor, outdoor, rooftop and container installations have distinct requirements; no location is universally best.

Coordinate insurer approval and fire department review before committing. Provide operator training, inspections, authorized shutdown/response procedures and vendor contacts. Do not open cabinets, bypass interlocks or attempt electrical repairs. This is not incident guidance; follow site procedures and emergency services.

Use qualified removal, transport and recycling providers following waste, transport and environmental rules, with special handling where needed for damage. EPA considers most discarded lithium ion batteries likely hazardous for ignitability or reactivity, not ordinary trash; see its commercial recycling guidance . Contracts must assign cleanup, restoration, financial security and surviving obligations. Warranties do not fund decommissioning.

## What belongs in a battery lease or ownership agreement?

Energy and property counsel should distinguish purchase, equipment and service, tenant improvement and ground lease rights. Identify the equipment owner, operator and utility account holder; installation does not confer every responsibility.

- Site rights: equipment footprint, access, cables, drainage, utility easements, maintenance areas and restoration; preserve truck courts and expansion plans.
- Economics: fixed/variable payments, development option rent, milestones, savings measurement, baselines, escalation, charges and dispatch obligations.
- Approvals and operations: permit/interconnection responsibility, costs, commissioning, inspections, data access, remote control security, downtime and notices.
- Risk allocation: insurance, indemnities, pollution/cleanup duties, casualty, neighbor impacts, defaults, parent support and required security.
- Transfers and endings: lender consent, assignment, sale, tenant expiration, equipment liens, casualty termination, removal deadlines and decommissioning security.

Check fire/property, interruption, liability and environmental coverage and exclusions; standard landlord policies may not suffice. Confirm lender liens, collateral, consent and remedies. Non disturbance/access agreements must protect existing lease and lender rights.

BESS does not automatically raise appraised value; buyers may discount short warranties, unfavorable contracts, restricted land, contingent revenue or removal costs. Long storage leases can support income but reduce flexibility. Retirement planning needs developer credit, operations and marketability review, not rent alone.

## An owner checklist from proposal through end of life

- Define the objective: bill reduction, solar use, critical load resilience or land rent, with measurable priorities and no conflicting assumptions.
- Establish the baseline: bills, interval data, operations, outages, tenant/meter rights and equipment/service constraints.
- Screen the site: title, leases, lender, utility, engineer, fire officials, insurer and zoning before equipment orders.
- Compare proposals: usable delivered power/energy, end of life performance, system certification/test evidence, full costs and controls.
- Model adverse cases: smaller savings, changed tariff, tenant departure, degradation, downtime, delayed approvals and removal costs.
- Document contracts: guarantees and their conditions, measurable service levels, approved operating modes, data rights and security.
- Commission professionally: retain approved plans, permits, utility authorization, acceptance records, warranties and operating/emergency documents.
- Monitor and maintain: reconcile results with the baseline, maintain logs and support, and update plans when operations or tenants change.
- Plan the exit: transfers, lender rights, lease expiry, augmentation, recycling, removal and restoration funding.

Capacity is not feasibility. Retain a complete file for future owners, tenants, lenders and managers, independent of the salesperson.

## 20 questions industrial owners ask about BESS

### What does B.E.S.S. stand for?

B.E.S.S., usually BESS, means battery energy storage system: batteries, power conversion, controls, thermal management, protection and site equipment that store and later deliver electricity.

### Does a BESS generate electricity?

No. It stores permitted grid or onsite generation. Charging, conversion and auxiliary losses mean less energy is delivered than charged at comparable measurement boundaries.

### What is the difference between kW and kWh?

kW measures power; kWh measures energy. Both instantaneous output and usable delivered energy must meet the load and duration. Nominal capacity alone does not establish runtime.

### Do I need solar panels to use battery storage?

No. Systems may charge from the grid under utility/tariff rules. Adding solar requires project specific review of compatibility, controls, exports and economics.

### Will a grid connected battery automatically power my warehouse during an outage?

No. Backup requires engineered utility isolation, suitable equipment/controls, approved protection and defined loads. Many bill management systems cannot island; whole building backup is not implicit.

### Can a battery back up my entire manufacturing facility?

Only if the approved design supports its power, starting surges, duration and operations. An engineer must assess loads and outage goals; critical load backup may be more practical.

### How does a BESS reduce demand charges?

Discharging during chargeable peaks can reduce grid demand if power, duration and controls match the tariff/load. Ratchets, peak windows and recharging can erase savings. Use interval data.

### Does battery storage always lower electricity bills?

No. Tariffs, peaks, charging costs, losses, controls, degradation and project costs determine savings. Flat rates or unsuitable loads may offer little benefit. Compare supported simulations with cheaper efficiency/scheduling options.

### How long does a commercial battery last?

Life varies with chemistry, temperature, cycling, throughput, operating limits and maintenance. Review capacity/service warranties, end of life performance, replacement costs and financial assumptions.

### Can I sell stored electricity back to the grid?

Only with applicable permissions, interconnection, metering and commercial arrangements. Technical capability establishes neither export rights nor payment rates. Retail and wholesale processes differ.

### Does a nonexport system avoid utility review?

No automatic exemption applies. Parallel connected equipment may still need review, protection, studies and approval. Confirm current utility requirements and configuration before purchase or operation.

### Can I put a BESS in an unused truck court or warehouse corner?

Only after site, code, fire, utility, lease and insurer review. Check access, trucks, drainage, exits, neighbors and electrical constraints. Vacant areas may serve circulation or have easement restrictions.

### Are lithium ion storage systems free of fire risk?

No. Thermal runaway can release heat/gases, spread or reignite. Professional design, suitable equipment, code compliance, maintenance and emergency planning reduce but do not eliminate hazards.

### Are UL 9540 and UL 9540A the same approval?

No. UL 9540 addresses system safety certification; UL 9540A tests thermal runaway fire propagation. Evidence must match the configuration and neither replaces permits nor establishes universal safety.

### Does meeting NFPA 855 guarantee a permit?

No. Officials apply locally adopted codes, editions and amendments to each project. Utility, zoning, building and fire approvals are separate; additional documentation may be required.

### Who receives savings when the tenant pays the electric bill?

The account and lease generally govern benefit allocation. Landlord spending does not automatically create savings or NOI. Agree on meter access, payments, baselines and responsibilities before installation.

### Is leasing land for a grid battery the same as installing onsite storage?

No. Developers usually operate separate projects; landlords receive contractual rent, not automatic energy revenue or cheaper power. Review credit, options, easements, interconnection and removal obligations.

### Will BESS automatically raise my building's value?

No. Buyers/lenders assess documented net benefits, condition, warranties, contracts and removal costs. Land restrictions, short support terms or unfavorable agreements can offset gains.

### Does every commercial battery qualify for rebates or tax credits?

No. Law/program terms, equipment, ownership, timing and other conditions govern eligibility. Get utility/tax advice before purchase; model conditional incentives separately from committed funding.

### Who pays to remove batteries when the project ends?

Contracts should assign removal, lawful handling, recycling, cleanup and restoration with financial security. Tenants, developers or manufacturers may lack funds when obligations arise.

# Commercial property owner questions: income, costs and decisions

Educational, not an appraisal or investment, tax, legal, engineering or insurance advice. Verify your property, leases and current rules with qualified advisers.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Answers and sources for commercial-property decisions, emphasizing 10,000-100,000-SF industrial buildings across nine Illinois counties.
- Document income before valuing it.
- Expense cuts must preserve safety, condition and lease obligations.
- Tax appeals and insurance renewals have their own evidence and deadlines.
- No guide can supply a universal rent, return, premium or reserve target.
- Owner lens: Treat owner time, related-party services, deferred work, and unpaid tenant charges as real economic costs when judging performance, even if they do not appear consistently in the property statement.

## Income, value and cash-flow questions

NOI: definition, inclusions, recoveries and worked statement explains operating income; DCF: projections, present value and exit sensitivity models it through a hold; investment diligence and calculators connects it to price and debt.

The CRE retirement guide separates spendable property cash from account distributions and covers IRA/401(k) restrictions, liquidity, sales or exchanges, Illinois taxes and succession.

The CRE tax and inheritance guide answers 35 retiree questions on lazy 1031, passive-loss offsets, cost segregation, depreciation, recapture, Illinois tax and inherited basis. Federal and state rules differ; a deduction does not guarantee more spendable cash.

## Operating costs, insurance and tax questions

Cost controls covers energy, maintenance and CAM; owner insurance covers limits, valuation and renewals; Illinois property taxes covers assessment, appeals and Cook incentive classes. Budgets, reserves and capital separates cash needs from accounting and tax treatment.

## Prepare the next owner decision

Before renewal, refinancing or sale, gather rent roll, lease abstracts, trailing statements, arrears, tax notices, policy schedules, contracts, condition reports and capital plan. Test operating downside before committing value or payout. Use the lease guide , selling guide and due-diligence checklist .

Cook, DeKalb, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake, McHenry and Will have different records and calendars. Use the county research directory to find the authority; a Chicago address label does not establish jurisdiction.

## Owner questions and answers

### How is NOI calculated for commercial real estate?

Subtract vacancy and credit loss from potential rent, add collectible recoveries and other property income to get EGI, then subtract property operating expenses. Keep debt, depreciation and major capital cash needs separate. Read the detailed guide .

### What is a good NOI?

No universal amount or margin exists. Compare period, use, leases, occupancy, condition and reserve convention consistently, supporting future changes with evidence. Read the detailed guide .

### What is included in operating expenses?

Real estate taxes, property insurance, owner-paid utilities, recurring repairs, maintenance and management are common categories. Recoveries and exclusions depend on leases; capital and financing are separate. Read the detailed guide .

### How can I lower commercial property taxes in Illinois?

Check parcel characteristics and assessment evidence; meet the correct assessor or Board deadlines. After county review, discuss PTAB or court options with counsel. Assessment reductions do not guarantee proportional bill reductions. Read the detailed guide .

### How can I reduce CAM charges?

Remove waste, compare equivalent vendor scopes, verify invoices and allocate only lease-permitted costs. Review caps, exclusions, audit rights and reconciliation timing instead of shifting disputed costs to tenants. Read the detailed guide .

### How can I lower commercial building insurance costs?

Document risk improvements and accurate values, compare equivalent quotes and review deductibles with a licensed adviser. A cheaper premium is not a saving if it removes required or important protection. Read the detailed guide .

### When should I use DCF instead of just a cap rate?

DCF is useful when lease rollover, capital spending or changing income matters during the hold. Direct capitalization is a one-year snapshot. Both require supported inputs and a consistent cash-flow basis. Read the detailed guide .

### How can I increase commercial property value?

Improve durable collected income, accurate recoveries, building condition and leasing certainty while controlling waste. The value effect depends on risk, future costs and supported pricing assumptions; no fixed uplift is guaranteed. Read the detailed guide .

### When should I sell an industrial building?

Compare holding, refinancing and selling after reviewing lease expirations, capital needs, debt maturity, tax basis and your liquidity/goals. Prepare the document file and review tax planning before committing to a sale. Read the detailed guide .

### How much should I reserve for repairs and vacancy?

Build a property-specific schedule of capital work, leasing costs, deductibles, carrying costs and debt maturity. Separate restricted lender reserves from usable cash; no universal percentage guarantees adequacy. Read the detailed guide .

### Does a triple-net lease eliminate owner expenses?

No. Contract exclusions, caps, vacancy, owner obligations and uncollected reimbursements can leave costs with the landlord. Read the signed lease rather than relying on the NNN label. Read the detailed guide .

### What are DSCR, LTV and debt yield?

DSCR compares defined income to debt service; LTV compares debt to a lender's value basis; debt yield compares a defined NOI to loan balance. Lenders set their own conventions and requirements. Read the detailed guide .

### Is a repair an expense or a capital improvement?

Scope and accounting and tax rules control. Maintenance and major replacements often differ; IRS rules examine betterments, restorations and adaptations. Ask a CPA, not just the invoice amount. Read the detailed guide .

### Can a 1031 exchange remove all taxes from a sale?

No. A qualifying exchange can defer eligible gain; cash, nonqualifying property, ownership and timing issues may create tax. Consult a CPA, attorney and qualified intermediary before closing. Read the detailed guide .

### Are ComEd and Nicor savings programs available to every building?

No. Utility territory/account, project type, equipment, program funding and application conditions matter. Check the official utility program before purchase; incentives and savings are not guaranteed. Read the detailed guide .

# How is net operating income calculated for commercial property?

Educational, not an appraisal or investment, tax, legal, engineering or insurance advice. Verify your property, leases and current rules with qualified advisers.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

NOI measures property operations, not cash in the bank. Reconcile leases, collections, expenses and recoveries on a consistent annual basis.
- Effective gross income minus property operating expenses equals NOI.
- Debt service, depreciation, owner income taxes and capital spending are not ordinary NOI expenses.
- A lease recovery is income to the owner, not permission to hide the matching expense.
- Compare trailing, current and stabilized NOI separately.
- Owner lens: When comparing an owner-occupied building with an investment, show a supportable market rent for the occupied space and keep business costs separate from property expenses; otherwise the comparison can overstate or understate NOI.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_Warehouses in Elk Grove Village, Illinois. Separate property operating income from debt service, owner income taxes and major capital spending._

## What is NOI, and what is included?

Net operating income = effective gross income (EGI) minus operating expenses. Start with full-occupancy rent on the chosen lease or market basis, less vacancy, free rent and collection losses, plus other property income and recoveries. Reconcile rent roll, signed amendments, receivables and ledger.

Typical expenses are real estate taxes, building insurance, owner-paid utilities, repairs, maintenance, contracted services and management. When comparing professionally managed investments, include a supported management allowance even if the owner self-manages. Owner business revenue, tenant sales, refundable deposits and loan proceeds are not property rental income.

NOI usually excludes mortgage principal and interest, depreciation, owner income taxes, acquisition costs, tenant improvements, leasing commissions and major capital replacements. Replacement reserves may sit below NOI or enter a lender-adjusted measure. State and reconcile the convention; do not compare incompatible figures.

## NOI calculation: a worked rent-to-income example

Hypothetical annual illustration, not market rent, expense benchmarks or an actual transaction. No property size or market performance is implied.

**Annual operating statement illustration**
- Step: Amount: Treatment
- Gross potential base rent: $400,000: Full scheduled rent on the stated basis
- Vacancy and credit loss: ($20,000): One combined illustrative allowance, not double-counted
- Expense recoveries: $80,000: Collectible reimbursements under leases
- Other property income: $5,000: Documented ancillary charges
- Effective gross income: $465,000: $400,000 - $20,000 + $80,000 + $5,000
- Operating expenses: ($145,000): Taxes $75,000; insurance $15,000; utilities $10,000; repairs/services $30,000; management $15,000
- NOI: $320,000: $465,000 - $145,000

With $180,000 annual debt service and $40,000 separate capital spending, cash after both is $100,000, not $320,000. It still excludes income taxes, leasing costs and other owner cash needs. Test assumptions with the existing cap-rate and debt-service calculators .

## How do NNN, modified-gross and gross leases change NOI?

For triple-net leases, record recoverable taxes, insurance and maintenance as expenses and collectible reimbursements as income, deducting the unrecovered share. “NNN” does not define eligible repairs, capital items, administration or reassessment increases.

Gross leases leave more expense risk with the owner; modified gross may use a base year, expense stop or negotiated split. Check each tenant’s exclusions, caps, gross-up clauses, audit rights and reconciliation deadlines. A vacant suite may not reimburse its share. See lease expense allocation and CAM reconciliation and cost controls .

## How do buyers and lenders re-underwrite NOI?

Separate trailing-12-month results, a forward annual estimate and stabilized NOI. Buyers may remove one-time income, replace related-party service costs with supported costs, normalize maintenance, adjust management fees, budget insurance renewal and test future Illinois taxes. No adjustment is automatic; retain its evidence and effective date.

After lease expiry, model downtime, tenant improvements and commissions. Stabilized NOI at full occupancy is not current collected income. The DCF guide models costs through a hold; the Illinois tax guide covers reassessment and appeals.

### Common mistakes that inflate NOI
- Counting recoveries without the matching expense.
- Ignoring free rent, arrears, nonrecoverable CAM or approaching vacancy.
- Calling a major roof replacement routine maintenance.
- Treating a low historical tax bill as guaranteed.
- Mixing cash and accrual reporting or area denominators without reconciliation.

## What is a good NOI, and how does it affect value?

No universal “good” NOI or margin exists. Compare type, condition, leases, occupancy and reporting convention, not totals alone for a 10,000-SF gross-leased building versus a 100,000-SF net-leased warehouse.

Direct capitalization uses value = NOI / supported cap rate. Durable NOI may increase indicated value, but vacancy risk, lease term, functionality and capital needs affect the rate and buyer adjustments. Owner-paid energy savings fully reimbursed by a tenant may lower tenant costs without adding owner NOI. Improve budget discipline and reserves , not promise a fixed uplift.

## Owner questions and answers

### Does NOI include mortgage payments?

No. Principal and interest are financing cash flows below ordinary NOI; lenders may adjust income for debt sizing.

### Is a roof replacement deducted from NOI?

A major replacement is generally a capital cash need presented separately from NOI; routine repair treatment depends on the work and accounting convention. Tax classification is a separate CPA review.

### What is a good NOI for a commercial property?

There is no universal figure. Compare documented income and expenses on the same period, occupancy, lease and reserve basis, then consider condition and future leasing costs.

# DCF explained for commercial real estate owners

Educational, not an appraisal or investment, tax, legal, engineering or insurance advice. Verify your property, leases and current rules with qualified advisers.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Discounted cash flow (DCF) values future property receipts and costs today, exposing lease rollover, uneven capital work and changes hidden by cap-rate snapshots.
- Project income, expenses and capital cash needs year by year.
- An exit cap rate converts future NOI into a resale estimate; a discount rate converts future cash into present value.
- Unlevered cash flows exclude debt; levered equity cash flows include it.
- Sensitivity is more useful than a single optimistic IRR.
- Owner lens: For an owner-user, separate the building investment from the operating business: compare ownership with a realistic lease alternative and include moving, downtime, fit-out, and eventual disposition costs.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_Industrial properties in Elk Grove Village, Illinois. Model each asset’s cash flow and test lease, capital, financing and exit assumptions._

## How do you build a property cash-flow projection?

Set valuation date and hold period. Project tenant rent, options and expirations; separate recoveries, taxes, insurance, repairs and management. Model rollover retention or vacancy, downtime, free rent, supported new rent, tenant improvements (TI) and leasing commissions (LC). Do not count the same vacancy loss in reduced rent and a separate deduction.

Property cash flow is more than NOI : subtract capital replacements and leasing costs when incurred, and state reserve treatment. In a 10,000-100,000-SF building, one tenant departure or roof project can dominate a year. Use condition reports and lease abstracts, not a universal rent-growth rate.

Unlevered cash flow excludes financing. Equity models add acquisition loan proceeds, subtract hold-period debt service and deduct sale payoff and finance charges. Match discount rates and return labels to cash flows; separate pre-tax and after-tax models.

## Discount rate versus cap rate: what is the difference?

Discount rates value future cash today at an assumed required return. Cap rates divide one year’s income by value. Exit caps assume resale, commonly using next-year stabilized NOI at hold’s end. These rates are neither interchangeable nor necessarily equal.

For end-of-year cash flow, present value = cash flow / (1 + discount rate) year . Net present value (NPV) subtracts the initial investment from discounted receipts. Positive NPV means the modeled investment exceeds the chosen return requirement on these assumptions, not that the outcome is certain.

IRR is the rate that makes NPV zero. Later negative outlays can produce multiple or unhelpful IRRs; dated cash flows also differ from simple annual periods. Keep NPV, required capital and downside exposure visible even when IRR looks attractive.

## DCF worked example: operating cash, reversion and present value

Illustration only, not market data, an appraisal or an investment recommendation. Assumptions: three-year unlevered hold, end-of-year receipts, no income taxes and an 8% discount rate.

**Assumed annual dollars; capital and leasing cash outlays below NOI**
- Year: NOI: Capital / TI / LC: Operating cash
- 1: $200,000: $50,000: $150,000
- 2: $210,000: $30,000: $180,000
- 3: $220,000: $30,000: $190,000

Assume year-4 NOI of $230,000 and a 7% exit cap. Gross year-3 reversion = $230,000 / 0.07 = $3,285,714.29; after assumed 2% sale costs, net reversion is $3,220,000. Year-3 total cash is $3,410,000, including $190,000 operating cash. Year-4 NOI prices the sale but is not received again during the hold.

Present value = $150,000 / 1.08 + $180,000 / 1.08 2 + $3,410,000 / 1.08 3 = $3,000,177.82 . With $3,000,000 all-in initial investment, NPV is $177.82; at $3,100,000, NPV is negative $99,822.18. Results depend entirely on assumptions and cash timing.

## How do exit cap, rent and downtime change the result?

At $230,000 year-4 NOI, illustrative gross resale is $3,833,333 at a 6% exit cap, $3,285,714 at 7% and $2,875,000 at 8%, rounded to dollars before sale costs. A higher exit cap lowers resale at the same income. None is a Chicago market claim.

Model discount/exit-rate combinations and a separate operating downside: lower collected rent, higher tax and insurance, longer downtime, larger TI/LC, capital overruns and delayed sale. Rent growth and a lower exit cap are not guaranteed benefits. In a levered case, include refinancing maturity and required additional equity, not just revised return.

Direct capitalization is a useful NOI/cap-rate snapshot for stabilized income. DCF exposes changes and execution costs, but detail cannot make speculative assumptions reliable. Have an appraiser and financial/tax advisers review property-specific inputs and conventions.

## Owner questions and answers

### Is the discount rate the same as the cap rate?

No. A discount rate values a series of future cash flows; a cap rate relates one year of NOI to value. An exit cap rate is a future resale assumption.

### Does a high IRR prove a good real estate investment?

No. Cash timing and assumptions drive IRR; nonconventional flows can mislead. It does not measure absolute capital at risk. Review NPV, required equity and downside.

### Should DCF include mortgage payments?

Include debt service and loan payoff in a levered equity model, not in an unlevered property model. Match the discount rate to the cash-flow basis.

# Free commercial property DCF and investment calculator

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## Start with your assumptions

Model income, expenses, debt, capital costs and a sale over a one-to-ten-year hold. Compare NOI, cap rate , cash-on-cash, IRR, NPV and equity multiples without sending your inputs to a server.

The calculator begins blank. The optional example is hypothetical, not market data, a recommended rate or a real property. Entries stay in this page's memory; reload clears them. No login, property database or calculator API is used.

## What formulas does this DCF calculator use?

Effective gross income (EGI) = scheduled rent - vacancy/credit loss + percentage rent + other income + recoveries.

Standard NOI = EGI - operating expenses - management fees - property taxes - insurance. This tool's reserve-adjusted NOI also deducts the separately entered replacement reserve. Do not compare it with a reserve-free broker or lender NOI without reconciling the convention.

GRM = price / annual scheduled rent. Cap rate = year-one reserve-adjusted NOI / price.

Initial equity = price + closing costs - loan + upfront interest reserve. Cash-on-cash = (year-one reserve-adjusted NOI - debt service) / initial equity, before income tax and one-time capital events.

Monthly payment = principal × monthly rate / [1 - (1 + monthly rate) -number of payments ]. At a zero rate, payment = principal / number of payments. Interest-only periods are in years; principal amortization begins afterward.

DSCR = reserve-adjusted NOI / annual debt service. Debt yield = reserve-adjusted NOI / initial loan. LTV = loan / price.

Gross sale value = annualized sale-month reserve-adjusted NOI / exit cap rate. Net sale proceeds deduct selling costs, outstanding debt and modeled exit taxes. A shortfall stays negative; a refinance or balloon payoff can also require extra cash.

Total equity cash flow = reserve-adjusted NOI - TI - LC - additional capex - debt service + reserve draw + gross refinance proceeds - refinance payoff - refinance costs - operating tax + net sale proceeds. LP and sponsor distributions allocate this total; they are not subtracted again from the total-equity return.

NPV = sum of cash flow in year t / (1 + discount rate) t , starting at t = 0. IRR is a rate at which NPV equals zero. Equity multiple = net cash returned over the hold / initial investment. Negative contributions reduce the net-cash multiple. IRR may be undefined or have multiple roots when signs change repeatedly.

Unlevered returns run the model again without borrowing, loan payoff or refinancing, rather than treating leveraged sale proceeds as debt-free cash. Both annual IRRs use end-of-year timing; monthly viewing does not turn them into monthly IRRs. The grid displays whole dollars; internal growth and loan formulas use full precision.

## What should owners verify before using the results?

This is education, not investment, tax, legal or insurance advice . Pavlo Rospopa provides this free planning tool; outputs are not appraisals, lender approvals or forecasts. Review leases, budgets and tax treatment with the appropriate professionals.

Annual growth compounds monthly. The model sells in the selected month and stops operating cash flows then. It uses annualized sale-month NOI, not forward-year NOI, and a simplified lease-renewal probability with downtime and renewal TI/LC. It does not implement a full new-tenant leasing strategy, real lease CAM reconciliation, tax-return calculations or all entity-specific rules. Fields labeled Reference are kept for comparison with the former workspace form but do not independently change cash flows.

Tax modeling is deliberately simplified: principal payments and reserve deposits are not income-tax deductions; interest and illustrative building depreciation are used. The 39-year convention, assumed bonus allocation, loss usage, recapture, installment-sale percentage and 1031 toggle are planning assumptions, not determinations of eligibility, law or timing. A full 1031 toggle assumes complete exit-tax deferral without checking qualification. A CPA must review these inputs and any modeled loss benefit.

The LP/sponsor allocation returns LP capital, then pays accrued preferred return, then a simplified sponsor catch-up and promote. It is not a partnership agreement. Total-equity IRR is different from the return to an individual LP or sponsor. Reference-only GP ownership does not implement a separate GP capital-return tier.

Use the NOI guide , DCF assumptions guide and budget and reserve planning to reconcile inputs. Do not enter sensitive personal or property information on a shared device.

# How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?

Educational, not an appraisal or investment, tax, legal, engineering or insurance advice. Verify your property, leases and current rules with qualified advisers.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Cut waste without creating larger repair, compliance, vacancy or tenant-retention costs. Start with documented bills, scopes and lease obligations.
- Start with invoices, meter use, service scope and lease responsibility.
- Compare total cost and risk, not only the lowest bid.
- Check utility-program eligibility before ordering work.
- Savings and tenant recoveries affect owner NOI differently.
- Owner lens: Count a proposed saving only after checking lease permissions, safety and code duties, insurer requirements, service reliability, and implementation cost; document a before-and-after baseline.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_Photovoltaic panels on the Rose Calendars factory roof. Evaluate energy projects against actual bills, equipment condition and lease responsibilities._

## Which operating costs should an owner review first?

Collect at least a year of bills and contracts. Separate recurring expenses, one-time repairs, capital replacements and tenant payments. Compare relevant area, consumption, hours and occupancy; heated manufacturing and unheated storage costs are not comparable. See budgeting and normalized expense comparisons .

Track actions, responsible parties, implementation costs, supported benefits, lease recoveries, approvals and results. Check duplicate invoices, incorrect meters, vacant-area services, expired promotions and auto-renewals. Charges are not automatically tenant-recoverable.

## How can industrial owners reduce energy and utility waste?

Review interval electricity, demand charges, seasonal gas, supply and delivery costs. Confirm utility tariffs; cheaper commodity quotes may hide fees or unfavorable renewals. Demand savings depend on peak timing, not annual kilowatt-hours alone.

Ask qualified contractors about LEDs and controls, occupancy scheduling, office HVAC setpoints, dock seals and weather-stripping. Match controls to tasks, hours and equipment. Preserve required emergency lighting, ventilation, fire and freeze protection. Check water/sewer bills for leaks, irrigation timing, meter errors and locally permitted adjustments; sewer charges do not simply disappear.

Check the official ComEd business savings portal and Nicor Gas business efficiency resources . Offers depend on account, territory, measure and current rules. Before purchase, confirm eligibility, approved equipment, preapproval, deadlines and whether landlord or tenant applies. No rebate, approval or savings percentage is promised.

Simple payback = net project cost / supported annual savings. Include installation, commissioning, disruption and maintenance; count rebates only if eligible and approved. A project may lower tenant costs or improve resilience without immediately increasing owner NOI.

## Preventive maintenance versus deferred repairs

Track roof sections, HVAC, docks, pavement, drains and life-safety systems by condition, warranty, maintenance responsibility and next inspection. Qualified inspections can distinguish repair from replacement and schedule work around tenants. Deferring leaks or clogged drains can increase damage, not save money.

Use a multi-year roof, HVAC and paving plan; compare scopes, restoration, permit responsibilities and warranties. Do not cut required fire-system testing, access, structural repairs or worker safety. Engineering and municipal requirements govern the work.

## How do service rebids and management fees reduce waste?

Rebid waste, landscaping, snow, janitorial, security and maintenance at identical service levels. Specify frequency, disposal fees, after-hours response, snow triggers, de-icing, insurance, reporting and escalation. A low bid may cost more if it excludes emergencies or transfers uninsured risk.

Compare management fee bases and services, not percentages alone: collections, reporting, lease administration, capital supervision and extras. Check invoice approvals and related-party vendors. Calendar renewals before cancellation windows close.

## How can an owner reduce CAM disputes and improve recoveries?

For each lease, record pro rata share and area basis, included costs, exclusions, caps, management fees, capital-amortization permissions, gross-ups, expense stops, reconciliation deadline and audit rights. Allocate once, keep invoices, reconcile estimates to permitted actual costs, return credits and explain increases.

Reduce CAM by removing waste and billing accurately, not shifting excluded costs. Caps or vacant shares may leave savings with either party. Show expense reductions and lower recoveries in the NOI bridge before claiming a benefit. Have counsel review disputed clauses and changes.

For major cost categories, see the Illinois property-tax appeal and budgeting guide and insurance renewal/risk checklist ; their deadlines, evidence and trade-offs differ from vendor bids.

## A repeatable cost-control cycle
- Record the baseline bill, service scope and owner/tenant allocation.
- Get comparable proposals and approvals before changing service.
- Track implementation cost separately from approved incentives.
- Compare later consumption and invoices, adjusting for weather or occupancy where relevant.
- Reconcile recoveries and update the next budget.

Illustrative arithmetic, not a forecast: a $6,000 annual invoice reduction less $2,000 unreimbursed implementation cost yields $4,000 first-year net cash before other effects. If tenants reimburse the full recurring expense, owner NOI may not rise by $6,000.

## Owner questions and answers

### How do I reduce CAM charges without cutting essential service?

Audit scope, invoices and lease allocations; rebid comparable services and remove duplicate or ineligible charges. Do not cut required safety work or bill tenants for excluded costs.

### Do LED upgrades automatically qualify for ComEd incentives?

No. Confirm the account, measure, equipment and current program requirements, including any preapproval, before purchase or installation.

### Does every expense reduction increase property value?

No. Lower expenses can reduce reimbursements; service cuts can worsen risk or occupancy. Calculate net owner income and capital costs first.

## Primary sources and scope

- ComEd: business energy savings programs
- Nicor Gas: business savings and efficiency resources
- IRS: tangible property regulations, repairs and capitalization

Owner education · Chicagoland commercial and industrial

# Commercial property insurance: an owner renewal checklist

Educational, not an appraisal or investment, tax, legal, engineering or insurance advice. Verify your property, leases and current rules with qualified advisers.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Match coverage to the building, tenancy and loss exposure. Comparing premiums without limits, exclusions, valuation and deductibles can leave an owner underinsured.
- Market purchase price is not the cost to rebuild the insured structure.
- Property, liability and business-income protection address different losses.
- Flood, earthquake and ordinance-or-law protection require explicit review.
- A certificate is evidence of insurance, not a substitute for policy endorsements.
- Owner lens: Coordinate insured replacement values, business-income limits and waiting periods, ordinance-or-law coverage, deductibles, lender terms, and lease obligations at renewal; a nominal limit alone does not establish claim adequacy.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_Inspectors review a building renovation in Vicenza, Italy. Conditions, protections and policy wording all matter to insurance review._

## What coverage should a commercial property owner discuss?

**Coverage questions for a licensed insurance adviser; not a policy recommendation**
- Coverage: Owner question
- Building/property: Which structures, permanently installed systems, perils and limits are insured? Are equipment breakdown and ordinance/law needs addressed?
- Business income / rental value: Does the form cover loss of rents after a covered loss, continuing expenses, waiting periods and the expected restoration period?
- General liability: Who is insured for premises-related liability, and what activities and exclusions matter?
- Umbrella / excess liability: Which underlying policies and limits must be maintained? Does the excess form leave gaps?
- Flood / earthquake: Are separate policies or endorsements needed? What are their limits, deductibles and exclusions?

Business-interruption or rental-value coverage does not guarantee ordinary default or vacancy protection. Check covered-loss triggers, waiting and restoration periods, and extensions. Landlord structures, tenant machinery and inventory, and each party’s liability may need separate policies.

FEMA says standard commercial property insurance typically excludes flood damage; NFIP commercial coverage excludes business-interruption or loss-of-use financial losses. Ask about private/excess options and gaps; flood building coverage does not necessarily protect rental income. Check the site and environmental diligence file and flood history.

## Replacement cost, ACV and coinsurance: why do they matter?

The Illinois Department of Insurance defines actual cash value (ACV) as replacement cost less depreciation for age and condition. Replacement cost covers like-kind/quality replacement without that deduction, subject to policy terms. Land, investment value and purchase price do not set the building’s reconstruction limit.

Review reconstruction estimates with a licensed adviser, considering area, construction, systems, location, debris removal and code upgrades. Confirm repair and replacement requirements, deadlines, recovery limits and sublimits.

Coinsurance requires a specified amount relative to policy valuation; underinsurance can reduce partial-loss payments. Confirm the contract’s percentage and ACV or replacement-cost basis, not a universal percentage or purchase-price penalty. Agreed-value provisions have conditions, not automatic protection.

## How should owners compare deductibles and exclusions?

Check whether deductibles are flat or percentage-based and what value the percentage uses. Wind/hail, flood, earthquake and water may have separate terms. Model cash exposure for multiple events, not just annual premium; lease reimbursements and lender rules may limit choices.

Review vacancy/unoccupancy conditions, sprinkler/alarm safeguards, roof limits, and contamination or wear exclusions. Tell the adviser about occupancy, stored commodities and operational changes. An older roof or changed tenant use warrants review, not a promised premium change.

## What should leases and tenant COIs require?

Have counsel and the licensed adviser coordinate limits, additional-insured status, waivers of subrogation, primary/noncontributory wording where appropriate, evidence deadlines and deductible responsibility. The lease and endorsed policy control; a certificate of insurance (COI) does not amend coverage.

Track policy-required renewal and cancellation information, verify entities and premises, and check contractor coverage before work. Tenant COIs do not insure owner buildings or replace owner liability protection. See lease allocation review when responsibilities are unclear.

## How can an owner manage commercial insurance premiums?
- Before renewal, prepare accurate building/use details, condition reports, loss runs and completed risk improvements.
- Ask qualified advisers about roof, drainage, fire protection, security and maintenance; get carrier feedback before spending for a hoped-for discount.
- Compare quotes at identical values, limits, deductibles, perils, income periods and exclusions; record differences.
- Check retained risk and lender/lease constraints before raising deductibles or removing coverage.
- Record the policy, endorsements, claims contacts and renewal date in the operating budget and reserve plan .

No premium benchmark or savings is promised. Building, use, history and insurer determine rates and coverage. Seek licensed recommendations; this is education, not insurance or legal advice.

## Owner questions and answers

### How can I lower commercial building insurance costs?

Improve risk information and maintenance, shop comparable coverage and review deductible options with a licensed adviser. Do not reduce required limits or silently remove protection to make a quote cheaper.

### Does commercial property insurance cover flooding and lost rent?

Do not assume it. Standard property policies typically exclude flood; NFIP commercial policies exclude business-interruption financial losses. Review separate flood and rental-value protection with an adviser.

### Should my building be insured for its purchase price?

Not automatically. Purchase price includes land and investment economics. The policy valuation basis and reconstruction exposure determine the insurance discussion.

- FEMA/NFIP: commercial flood coverage and exclusions

Owner education · Chicagoland commercial and industrial

# How to budget expenses, reserves and capital for a commercial building

Educational, not an appraisal or investment, tax, legal, engineering or insurance advice. Verify your property, leases and current rules with qualified advisers.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

A profitable operating statement may not fund a roof, vacant suite or loan maturity. Connect monthly operations, tenant recoveries, capital timing and financing without mixing them.
- Maintain an operating budget and a separate capital/liquidity plan.
- Normalize expense benchmarks for area, occupancy, use and lease basis.
- Reserves are cash set aside; spending and tax deductions are different events.
- Tax treatment is a separate CPA analysis, not an NOI shortcut.
- Owner lens: Keep unrestricted operating liquidity distinct from lender-controlled escrows and earmarked reserves. Stress near-term debt maturity and a major repair occurring in the same period as vacancy.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_National Park Service staff review plans at Cape Cod National Seashore. Prepare a documented capital and cash plan for the property; this is a reference photograph, not a client meeting._

## What belongs in a commercial operating budget?

Use invoices, signed leases and monthly trailing statements. Budget tenant base rent, recoveries, collection loss and ancillary income. Track taxes, insurance, utilities, repairs, snow, waste, grounds, management and recurring services; schedule renewals and seasonal bills by due date and compare annually.

For Chicagoland industrial assets, review winter service and heat, roof/drains, loading equipment and paving alongside tenancy. Separate tenant-paid utilities from landlord service. Include tax notices, appeal status and insurance-renewal assumptions instead of extrapolating a quiet year.

Monthly, reconcile budget and actual price, usage and timing, update collections and forecast. Tax refunds and insurance recoveries are not recurring income. NOI reconciliation preserves the operating basis; cash forecasts show liquidity timing.

## How do I benchmark operating expenses without misleading comparisons?

Define whether cost per square foot uses rentable, occupied or gross area. Compare property type, heated area, tenant use, service level, period and gross/net lease basis. Separate capital and one-time costs. Utility use per operating hour or occupied area may reveal more than dollars alone.

Use normalized history, comparable vendor scopes and verified peer data. This guide provides no Chicago expense ratios or market rates. A low ratio may reflect deferred maintenance, tenant-paid costs or missing management fees, not efficiency. Label sources and adjustments.

## Capex versus opex: where do roof and HVAC costs go?

**Separate owner reporting questions from tax classification**
- Item: Owner cash / underwriting view: Review needed
- Routine servicing: Typically recurring operating expense: Lease responsibility and accounting policy
- Major roof/system replacement: Separate capital plan and cash outlay: Condition, scope, permits and CPA classification
- TI and leasing commission: Leasing cash needs below ordinary NOI: Lease timing, amortization and tax treatment
- Reserve deposit: Cash earmarked for future needs, not the repair itself: Lender convention, funding and access restrictions

Federal IRS tangible-property rules distinguish ordinary expenses from capitalized amounts, including betterments, restorations and adaptations. Dollar size alone does not decide classification. Safe harbors and elections have conditions; do not relabel improvements as repairs to reduce NOI or taxable income.

## How much reserve cash does a commercial owner need?

No universal reserve percentage suffices. Schedule condition, timing, installed replacement estimates, lease responsibility and contingencies, plus vacancy carry, TI/LC, deductibles, tax timing and loan maturity. Separate lender-restricted reserves from readily available cash.

Illustrative arithmetic, not a reserve recommendation: a supported $120,000 project estimate, $20,000 already dedicated and five years to completion imply $20,000 annual straight-line funding before inflation, interest or contingencies. An earlier failure requires cash sooner. Do not count both annual contributions and the eventual project as expenses in the same cash-flow model.

## Depreciation, cost segregation and 1031: what should I ask my CPA?

Depreciation allocates eligible capital basis over its recovery period; it is not current-year cash spending and is excluded from ordinary property NOI. Land is not depreciable. Basis allocation, placed-in-service dates, classification, elections and current law matter. See IRS Publication 946 , not a promised deduction.

A cost-segregation study identifies supported components and tax classifications/recovery periods; it is neither an automatic percentage write-off nor an operating expense. Ask about study quality, basis reconciliation, timing, costs and recapture on sale. The IRS audit-guide directory links the Cost Segregation guide and warns that law may change after publication.

Section 1031 may defer, not erase, qualifying gain on business/investment real-property exchanges. Property held primarily for sale does not qualify; cash or other non-like-kind property may create taxable gain. Before closing, discuss ownership, qualified-intermediary arrangements, identification and completion deadlines, debt and state taxes. See sale/1031 preparation and the IRS real-estate exchange overview . Consult a CPA and attorney; no tax result is promised.

## Refinancing and debt costs belong in the liquidity plan

Track interest, amortization, fees, escrows, covenants, maturity, recourse and prepayment. DSCR compares a lender-defined income measure with debt service; LTV compares debt with its value basis; debt yield compares defined NOI with loan balance. No universal qualifying threshold applies.

Refinancing plans do not erase balloon balances. Test lower proceeds, higher borrowing costs and delayed closing; calculate cash gaps after payoff and fees. Use the debt-service calculator and financing guide and levered versus unlevered projections , not a duplicate calculator.

## Owner questions and answers

### What is included in commercial operating expenses?

Typically taxes, property insurance, owner-paid utilities, recurring repairs/services and management. Debt service, depreciation and major capital outlays are separate from ordinary NOI. State reserve and lease-recovery conventions.

### Are reserves the same as capital spending?

No. Reserves earmark cash; capital spending pays for work. Reconcile lender underwriting conventions to avoid double-counting.

### Does cost segregation increase NOI?

No. It concerns tax depreciation timing and classification, not rental operating income. Review eligibility, study quality, current law and later recapture with a CPA.

## Primary sources and scope

Official references checked 2026-10-06. Program terms, policy contracts, laws and local deadlines can change; use the linked office's current documents before acting. Examples on this page are educational assumptions, not local market data.
- IRS: tangible property regulations, repairs and capitalization
- IRS Publication 946: depreciation
- IRS: audit guides, including Cost Segregation Publication 5653
- IRS: like-kind exchanges of business/investment real estate
- OCC: Commercial Real Estate Lending handbook

## Connect tax deductions to retirement cash

Passive-loss rules can suspend a deduction even when a study shows a large first-year amount. Sale tax may include depreciation-related categories and Illinois adjustments. The CRE tax and retirement guide covers straight-line depreciation, cost segregation, current bonus rules, passive versus active offsets, recapture, lazy 1031 and inheritance. Use it to prepare for a CPA review, not to treat paper deductions as cash.

## Connect the budget with investment cash flow

Use the free budget-to-DCF calculator to separate operating costs, replacement reserves, TI, LC, capex and debt. Avoid entering detailed expense items again in a total that already includes them.

Lease comparison & preparation

# Comparing commercial leases in Chicago

No quoted market rents or available listings.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Compare total occupancy cost and operating fit for office, retail, industrial, warehouse and flex space, not just advertised rent. Lease language controls obligations.

- Compare total occupancy cost over the same term and area basis, not advertised rent.
- “Gross,” “modified gross,” and “NNN” are labels; the lease language assigns the actual expenses.
- Separate recurring, upfront, cash-tied-up, and contingent costs for every option.
- Confirm zoning, permits, and buildout timing before relying on a move-in date.
- Owner lens: For a landlord, define recoverable costs, caps, capital amortization, vacancy gross-ups, audit rights, and payment timing in the lease. Vacant space, disputed recoveries, and tenant credit still leave cash exposure with the owner.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_Dock positions, levelers, and trailer staging are lease terms as much as building features. Confirm who may use them and when._

## Gross and net are labels, not complete budgets

- **Gross lease**: Usually bundles some building expenses into rent; utilities, increases, exclusions and other charges may remain separate.
- **Modified gross lease**: Allocates expenses by agreement. Confirm what is included and what can change.
- **Net or triple-net (NNN) lease**: Adds taxes, insurance and maintenance to base rent, commonly. The label does not assign roof, structure, capital repairs or every operating cost.
- **Common area maintenance (CAM)**: Shared property costs; review the lease’s definition, allocation, exclusions, reconciliation and review rights.

Confirm whether the quoted rate is annual or monthly, its area basis and currency. Request the expense estimate and supporting history; actual pass-throughs may differ at reconciliation.

## Build a total occupancy-cost comparison

Separate recurring, upfront, refundable-security and later capital costs. Compare options over the same lease term and area basis, including scheduled increases.

- Recurring: base rent, tax and insurance pass-throughs, CAM, utilities, maintenance contracts, parking and other required charges.
- Upfront: professional review, permits, buildout, equipment installation, relocation and costs not reimbursed by a tenant-improvement allowance.
- Cash tied up: security deposits, prepaid rent and letters of credit. Refundable security ties up liquidity but is not automatically an operating expense.
- Contingent: expense increases, tenant-assigned major repairs, delayed delivery, exit restoration and costs of changing operations.

> Illustrative arithmetic only, not Chicago market data. If 10,000 rentable square feet were quoted at $12 per square foot per year in base rent and $4 in estimated annual pass-throughs, those two components would total $160,000 per year, or about $13,333 per month. Utilities, improvements, other charges, and future changes would still need to be added. This example is not an available property or a rent estimate.

Ask for each figure’s basis. Label unknowns as estimates and test a higher-cost case rather than treating them as zero.

_National Park Service staff review building plans at Cape Cod National Seashore. Document a lease’s buildout scope, delivery conditions and expense allocation._

## A lease-review checklist

- Premises and use: verify the space, shared areas, permitted use, parking, loading, yard rights and operating restrictions.
- Term and delivery: distinguish possession, rent commencement, substantial completion and conditions to operate.
- Improvements: document scope, approvals, allowance, reimbursement conditions, overruns, ownership and removal obligations.
- Repairs: allocate ordinary maintenance and major HVAC, roof, structural, pavement and fire-protection work.
- Expenses: review allocation percentages, exclusions, negotiated caps, reconciliation and document-review rights.
- Risk: have counsel review insurance, indemnity, casualty, condemnation, default remedies and any personal guaranty.
- Flexibility: check renewal options and notice deadlines, assignment, subleasing, expansion, termination and restoration.

An LOI organizes negotiations; wording and circumstances determine binding effect. Obtain counsel review before signing, rather than assuming all terms are nonbinding.

## Make the occupancy schedule credible

Check zoning and building requirements before setting a move-in date; allow for design, permits, utilities, construction, inspections and equipment commissioning. For industrial space, review loading, power, storage and fire-protection suitability early because each affects cost and timing.

Document deliverables, responsible parties, completion evidence and delay consequences. Confirm timing with authorities and contractors; “available now” does not mean business-ready.

## Sources and next steps

- Chicago zoning map : initial city zoning research; confirm the proposed use.
- Chicago Department of Buildings : permitting, inspection, and code resources.
- Cook County Treasurer : tax-bill verification when reviewing a Cook County property’s expense history.

Confirm jurisdiction and records with the property-research guide ; use the purchase-diligence guide if buying.

For industrial leases across county lines, use the nine-county Illinois industrial research hub to identify the authority and official records. Confirm use approvals, buildout responsibility and utility-upgrade timing before treating spaces as interchangeable.

For battery energy storage, agree on equipment ownership, meter access, savings allocation, maintenance, approvals, insurance, lender consent and removal at lease end. A landlord-funded battery does not automatically cut landlord costs when the tenant pays electricity. See the BESS lease and ownership checklist .

> General education only. Lease terms vary; obtain legal and financial advice for the specific lease and verify all cost assumptions.

## Continue with the owner guides

For the operating and financial questions behind this decision:
- How is net operating income calculated for commercial property?
- How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?
- Commercial property insurance: an owner renewal checklist
