Source: https://rospopa.com/resources/chicago-commercial-real-estate/
Published: 2026-10-02 · Updated: 2026-10-10

Research guide

# Researching Chicago commercial real estate

Educational guide, not a market report.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Start a commercial property search with your proposed use and a verification plan. An address, asking price and listing description cannot establish business or investment suitability.

- Start with use and verification, not an address or asking price.
- Identify the municipality, county, and every PIN; the zoning authority follows the parcel, not the mailing address.
- Confirm zoning maps, building records and tax bills with responsible authorities and qualified advisers.
- Compare options on the same basis: area definition, total cost, timing, and verified evidence.
- Owner lens: Before spending on a conversion, verify the approval path, who pays for utility or off-site work, and what happens to the budget if approvals or occupancy are delayed.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_Chicago’s Loop from the lakefront. City records cover the city; suburban and unincorporated parcels have their own authorities._

## 1. Define what the property must do

Record activity, occupancy date, usable area, budget and essential physical requirements, separate from preferences. For purchases, distinguish owner occupancy, rental income and redevelopment; underwriting differs.

- **Office**: Consider layout, accessibility, telecommunications, commuting and adaptation costs.
- **Retail and service space**: Check customer access, visibility, deliveries, permitted activity, licensing and buildout needs.
- **Industrial and warehouse property**: Evaluate loading, clear height, power, circulation and operations before comparing area. See the industrial evaluation guide .
- **Flex and mixed-use property**: Identify each actual use and its share. “Flex” does not establish permission for manufacturing, retail, laboratory or assembly.

## 2. Confirm the jurisdiction and parcel

“Chicago area” may mean the city or wider region. Identify municipality, county, address and every property index number (PIN). Marketing addresses may cover multiple parcels; mailing addresses do not establish zoning authority.

- For city property, start with Chicago zoning and building resources.
- For suburban property, check municipal planning and building departments; for unincorporated parcels, confirm the county authority.
- Use the parcel’s county assessor and treasurer. Cook County records do not cover DuPage, Lake, Will, Kane or other counties.

Log the source, retrieval date, parcel or address, result and open questions. Keep source documents, not just screenshots or search snippets.

The nine-county Chicagoland industrial hub links planning, zoning and parcel sources for Cook, DeKalb, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake, McHenry and Will, distinguishing county and municipal authority beyond the city.

## 3. Verify use, condition, and obligations

### Zoning is a starting point

Give the authority your zoning designation and proposed operation. Confirm approvals, special uses, parking, loading and restrictions. Existing occupancy or a prior business does not automatically permit a new operation.

### Building records need interpretation

Review available permits and violations; have qualified advisers investigate open issues. Public records may be incomplete and do not establish roof, structural, electrical, fire-protection or other conditions. Arrange inspections suited to the property and intended use.

### Taxes are not a fixed listing number

Match bills and assessments to the PINs and tax year. Assessed value, tax bill and market value are different. Ask a qualified tax adviser how reassessment, appeals, incentives or a use/ownership change may affect the budget; last year’s bill is not a forecast.

### Access and environmental questions can change the decision

Check access rights, easements, drainage and flood information. Past industrial activity may warrant environmental diligence even when current use appears ordinary. The purchase-diligence guide places these checks in acquisition review.

## 4. Put each option on the same basis

- Area: record the source and whether it is rentable, usable, building or land area.
- Cost: separate price or base rent from taxes, insurance, maintenance, utilities, improvements and transaction costs.
- Timing: include possession, approvals, construction and equipment installation, not just closing or lease dates.
- Evidence: distinguish verified facts from representations and estimates. Asking terms do not prove a completed transaction or market value.

Continue to comparing commercial leases for rentals or investment and purchase diligence for acquisitions.

## Official research sources

- City of Chicago zoning map : initial zoning location research; confirm interpretations with the responsible authority.
- Chicago Department of Buildings : building permits, inspections, and code-enforcement resources.
- Cook County Assessor : parcel and assessment research.
- Cook County Treasurer : tax bills and payment information.
- FEMA Flood Map Service Center : official flood-hazard maps, which do not show every water or drainage problem.

> This guide provides a research process, not a determination that any property is legal, safe, available, or suitable. Consult qualified legal, tax, design, and inspection professionals for the specific transaction.

## Related guides
- Industrial building suitability
- Commercial lease costs and obligations
- Investment purchase diligence

Published: 2026-10-03 · Updated: 2026-10-10

Reference · Industrial real estate and investment terms

# Industrial real estate & investment glossary

Plain-English reference for educational use.

By Pavlo Rospopa · Last updated October 10, 2026

## In brief

Decode industrial building, lease, underwriting, investment and Illinois records terms. These general definitions defer to contracts, statutes, ordinances and official records.

- Industrial terms span building features, contracts, accounting, and local records.
- A phrase can mean different things in a lease, appraisal, loan, survey, or zoning file.
- For Illinois records, verify the parcel, county, municipality, and official source.
- Term IDs provide stable links for search results and diligence notes.
- Owner lens: When records differ, rely on the controlling signed lease, loan, policy, survey, or government record.

## Talk about your building

Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap.

Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com

_Plan review at Cape Cod National Seashore. Keep the actual signed ownership, tax, improvement and valuation records for your property._

## Building & site

Physical features, site layout, and operating fit.

- **Clear height**: Usable vertical height from the finished floor to the lowest overhead obstruction.
- **Column spacing**: Distance between structural columns, affecting racking, staging, equipment and forklifts.
- **Dock-high door**: A loading door designed for trailers backed to a dock.
- **Drive-in door**: A grade-level overhead door that lets vehicles enter the building or yard area.
- **Truck court**: Paved area outside dock doors where trucks back, turn, and queue. Evaluate usable depth for the actual fleet and maneuver, not a universal turning radius. See the turning circle, swept-path, and offtracking reference .
- **Trailer parking**: Outdoor spaces used to store trailers, subject to zoning, surface, screening, and lease limits.
- **Cross-dock**: A building moving freight between inbound and outbound doors with little storage time.
- **Rail-served**: A property with rail access or a rail spur; service, rights, and track condition still need review.
- **ESFR sprinklers**: Early Suppression Fast Response sprinklers for certain high-piled storage conditions.
- **Slab load and flatness**: Slab capacity and surface tolerance, especially for heavy storage or narrow-aisle systems.
- **3-phase power**: Industrial electrical service; verify voltage, amperage, transformer capacity, and utility supply.
- **Mezzanine**: An intermediate platform or floor inside a building, subject to permits, structure, fire, and egress review.
- **Office finish %**: The portion of a building improved as office space.
- **Flex space**: A suite or building combining office, showroom, light industrial, storage, or service use.
- **IOS (industrial outdoor storage)**: Land for storing vehicles, equipment, materials, containers, or trailers. Permitted use depends on zoning, screening, surface, access, and environmental controls.
- **Class A/B/C industrial**: Informal market labels for relative quality, age, features, location, and tenant appeal.
- **Land-to-building ratio**: The relationship between site area and building area.
- **Site coverage**: The portion of a parcel covered by buildings and sometimes other impervious improvements.
- **Infill vs. greenfield**: Infill sites are in developed areas; greenfields are undeveloped or less-developed land.

## Leases

Lease language governs rent, expenses, risk, access, and remedies.

- **NNN / triple net**: A lease where the tenant commonly pays base rent, taxes, insurance, and operating expenses.
- **Gross lease**: A lease where many property expenses are included in rent.
- **Modified gross**: A lease between gross and net structures, with expenses allocated by contract.
- **CAM**: Common-area charges for costs such as snow, landscaping, lighting, security, pavement, and management, subject to lease inclusions, exclusions, caps, and allocation. See CAM reconciliation and cost controls .
- **Base rent**: Stated rent before pass-through expenses, credits, abatements, or other adjustments.
- **Escalations**: Scheduled rent increases or expense adjustments, fixed, percentage-based, index-based, or tied to operating costs.
- **TI allowance**: Money a landlord contributes toward approved tenant improvements.
- **LC (leasing commission)**: Compensation paid for procuring a tenant or lease renewal; model it as a leasing cash need in the hold-period DCF .
- **Expense stop**: A threshold where the landlord covers expenses up to a stated amount and the tenant pays certain increases above it.
- **Estoppel certificate**: A tenant statement confirming key lease facts, defaults, deposits, options, and claims.
- **SNDA**: Subordination, non-disturbance, and attornment agreement among tenant, landlord, and lender.
- **Holdover**: A tenant remaining after lease expiration, usually subject to lease consequences and remedies.
- **Renewal option**: Contractual right to extend a lease if notice, timing, and default conditions are met.
- **ROFR / ROFO**: Rights of first refusal or first offer that may affect sale or leasing flexibility.
- **WALT**: Remaining lease duration weighted by rent or area.
- **Rent roll**: Summary of tenants, suites, area, rent, deposits, options, and lease dates.

## Underwriting & investment

Check each investment term against the source model and period.

- **EGI (effective gross income)**: Potential rent less vacancy and credit losses, plus collectible recoveries and other property income, stated annually. See the rent-to-NOI bridge .
- **DCF (discounted cash flow)**: Projection discounting future property or equity cash flows to a valuation date. State capital, lease rollover, and sale assumptions. DCF guide .
- **NPV (net present value)**: Discounted future net receipts minus initial investment at a chosen rate; positive modeled NPV is not guaranteed. Worked example .
- **Discount rate**: Required return used to convert future cash to present value, matched to levered or unlevered and pre- or after-tax cash flows. Not a cap rate.
- **Exit cap rate**: Future resale capitalization assumption, commonly applied to the year after the hold's NOI. A higher rate lowers indicated resale at the same NOI.
- **Debt yield**: Defined annual NOI divided by loan balance; definitions and thresholds vary by lender. Financing comparison .
- **Capex (capital expenditures)**: Cash for capital improvements or replacements, generally modeled separately from property NOI. Tax capitalization is a separate analysis.
- **Opex (operating expenses)**: Recurring property operating costs on the stated accounting basis, such as taxes, insurance, maintenance and management. Debt service is separate.
- **Replacement reserve**: Cash earmarked for future capital needs; funding is not payment for work. State lender and model conventions to avoid double-counting.
- **Coinsurance**: A policy provision tying required insurance amounts to a specified value basis and percentage; underinsurance can reduce payment. Actual wording controls. Insurance valuation .
- **BI (business income) / loss of rents**: Insurance for qualifying income losses after a covered event, subject to triggers, time limits, and exclusions; not ordinary vacancy or tenant-default protection.
- **Cook County Class 6b**: An incentive assessment classification for qualifying industrial development, rehabilitation or reutilization, subject to application, local support and compliance. Compare incentive classes .
- **NOI**: Effective gross property income minus operating expenses, before debt service, depreciation, and major capital needs. State the reserve convention. See NOI calculation and recoveries .
- **Cap rate**: NOI divided by price or value; a shorthand income and risk measure, not a complete valuation.
- **Going-in vs. exit cap**: Going-in cap rate uses current or first-year income; exit cap rate is a resale assumption.
- **DSCR**: Debt service coverage ratio compares income available for debt payments to required debt service.
- **LTV**: Loan-to-value compares loan amount to property value, purchase price, or another lender-defined base.
- **IRR**: Internal rate of return is the discount rate that makes modeled net present value zero. Nonconventional cash flows may have multiple or no useful IRRs. See DCF return measures .
- **Equity multiple**: Total cash returned divided by total equity invested.
- **Cash-on-cash**: Annual cash flow compared with cash invested, often after debt service and before taxes.
- **Basis**: May mean tax basis, cost basis, or an investor's all-in cost. Confirm which definition applies.
- **Replacement cost**: Estimated cost to build a similar asset today.
- **Sale-leaseback**: A transaction where an owner sells a property and leases it back.
- **Owner-user vs. investor**: An owner-user buys to occupy; an investor buys for income, appreciation, redevelopment, or resale.
- **Value-add vs. core**: Core generally means stabilized assets with lower perceived risk; value-add involves vacancy, rollover, improvements, repositioning or other execution risk.
- **1031 exchange**: Qualifying exchange of business or investment real property that can defer gain. Deferred exchanges generally require identification within 45 days and completion by the earlier of 180 days or the relevant tax-return due date, including extensions, subject to detailed rules. See IRS Form 8824 instructions and owner tax planning . Consult a CPA or attorney before closing.
- **Qualified intermediary**: A party used to facilitate a 1031 exchange and hold exchange proceeds.
- **LOI**: A letter of intent outlining business terms before a purchase agreement or lease.
- **PSA**: A purchase and sale agreement governing price, deposits, diligence, conditions, default, and closing.
- **Due diligence period**: Agreed time for a buyer to inspect records, title, survey, environmental and physical condition, leases, zoning, and financing.
- **Earnest money**: A buyer deposit governed by the PSA and escrow instructions.

## Illinois & local records

Identify the correct county, municipality, township, and parcel.

- **PIN (property index number)**: A parcel identifier used in county tax and assessment records.
- **Assessed value & equalization factor**: Assessed value is the county’s property-tax figure, distinct from its underlying market value and the bill. County or Illinois Department of Revenue equalization factors standardize assessment levels across jurisdictions. Verify figures with the assessor and treasurer.
- **Triennial reassessment**: Cook County reassesses property on a three-year cycle; verify timing and notices with the county assessor.
- **Township assessor**: In most Illinois counties outside Cook, elected official who sets initial property values; the county supervisor of assessments reviews and equalizes them. Contact the county office to find the right township assessor.
- **Transfer tax**: A tax that may apply at state, county, or municipal levels when real estate changes ownership.
- **Zoning map amendment**: A legislative change to a parcel's zoning classification.
- **Special use**: A use allowed only after specific local approval, often with conditions.
- **Variance**: Relief from a zoning standard, such as a setback or parking requirement.
- **Unincorporated vs. incorporated**: Whether property is outside or inside municipal boundaries, affecting zoning, permits, services, and records.
- **Enterprise zone**: A designated area that may offer incentives if a project qualifies; eligibility must be verified.
- **TIF district**: A tax increment financing district that captures certain future tax growth for eligible public purposes.
- **Phase I ESA / AAI**: An environmental diligence report; EPA All Appropriate Inquiries guidance explains federal standards.
- **ALTA survey**: A detailed survey used to review boundaries, easements, improvements, access, and title-related survey matters.
- **Title commitment**: A title insurer's commitment to issue a policy subject to requirements and exceptions.

For broader local-record workflow, see the commercial property research guide and the nine-county industrial hub .

> This glossary is general education, not legal, tax, engineering, environmental, appraisal, brokerage, or investment advice. Definitions can change by contract, statute, ordinance, lender, or professional standard; verify property-specific meaning with qualified professionals and official sources.
